articles.title: Quem é o vice de Flávio Bolsonaro? | G1
articles.standfirst: Nascido em Maceió (AL), em 13 de agosto de 1970, Alfredo Gaspar tem 56 anos e já atuou como promotor de Justiça, advogado e professor universitário
articles.summary: Nascido em Maceió (AL), em 13 de agosto de 1970, Alfredo Gaspar tem 56 anos e já atuou como promotor de Justiça, advogado e professor universitário
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro e Alfredo Gaspar em Natal — Foto: Kléber Teixeira/Inter TV Cabugi

Alfredo Gaspar de Mendonça Neto ( PL ) é o candidato a vice-presidente do Brasil junto a Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Nascido em Maceió (AL), em 13 de agosto de 1970, Alfredo Gaspar tem 56 anos e já atuou como promotor de Justiça, advogado e professor universitário. Iniciou a carreira no Ministério Público de Alagoas aos 25 anos, onde trabalhou por mais de duas décadas.

No MP, atuou em promotorias criminais. Também foi procurador-geral de Justiça por dois períodos e presidiu o Grupo Nacional de Combate às Organizações Criminosas (GNCOC).

Se hoje está ao lado bolsonarismo, Alfredo Gaspar já foi próximo do senador Renan Calheiros ( MDB ) e do ex-governador Renan Filho (MDB), que foi ministros dos Transportes no governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ).

Em 2015, foi convidado por Renan Filho para assumir a Secretaria de Segurança Pública de Alagoas. Permaneceu no cargo até 2016, quando uma decisão do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) passou a impedir que membros do Ministério Público ocupassem funções políticas no Executivo sem deixar a carreira.

Em 2020, deixou definitivamente o MP para disputar seu primeiro cargo eletivo. Candidato à Prefeitura de Maceió pelo MDB, liderou no primeiro turno , mas foi derrotado por João Henrique Caldas , o JHC, na segunda etapa.

Após a eleição, voltou ao governo estadual para exercer novamente o cargo de secretário de Segurança Pública.

No início de 2022, rompeu politicamente com o grupo do então governador Renan Filho em meio à sucessão estadual.

Deixou o MDB, filiou-se ao União Brasil e concorreu à Câmara. Foi eleito deputado federal por Alagoas, figurando entre os parlamentares mais votados do estado e o mais votado da capital, Maceió. Em 2026, migrou para o PL, e passou a assumir o comando estadual da sigla .

A Polícia Federal recebeu um pedido de abertura de inquérito para investigar o deputado por suspeita de estupro de vulnerável. No entanto, o ministro Gilmar Mendes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), determinou o arquivamento da apuração.

O caso aconteceu durante um bate-boca na CPMI do INSS. Na ocasião, Lindbergh chamou Gaspar de “estuprador”. Gaspar respondeu chamando o petista de “bandido”. Relembre aqui.

Os processos têm como base declarações feitas pelos parlamentares, que são contestadas pelo deputado.

A indicação de Alfredo Gaspar para a chapa de Flávio Bolsonaro visa reforçar dois pilares estratégicos da campanha presidencial: o protagonismo da pauta de combate à criminalidade e a estruturação de um palanque competitivo no Nordeste.

A escolha de um nome ligado à carreira jurídica e com passado na segurança pública atende aos anseios da base conservadora, enquanto a atuação de Gaspar em Alagoas é vista no partido como peça para ampliar a penetração da candidatura em estados nordestinos.

articles.title: Professor Bira, geógrafo do IFBA, morre aos 51 anos em Salvador | G1
articles.standfirst: Ubiraci Carlúcio dos Santos tinha mais de 20 anos de experiência em sala de aula e contribuiu para projetos de valorização do patrimônio histórico e cultural da capital baiana.
articles.summary: Professor Bira, o geógrafo Ubiraci Carlúcio dos Santos, era docente do IFBA e referência na valorização do patrimônio histórico e cultural de Salvador.
articles.body:
Professor Bira, geógrafo e educador do IFBA, morre aos 51 anos em Salvador — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O professor e geógrafo Ubiraci Carlúcio dos Santos, conhecido como professor Bira, morreu na manhã desta terça-feira (20), aos 51 anos, em Salvador . A informação foi confirmada à produção da TV Bahia pela família, que optou por não divulgar a causa da morte.

Natural da capital baiana, Bira era formado em Geografia pela Universidade Federal da Bahia ( Ufba ), mestre em Educação pela Universidade do Estado da Bahia (Uneb) e professor do Instituto Federal da Bahia ( IFBA ).

Com mais de 20 anos de experiência em sala de aula, ele lecionou em pelo menos 40 instituições das redes pública e privada, em Salvador e no interior do estado. Também ministrava palestras em escolas públicas, organizações não governamentais, associações e sindicatos, com discussões sobre a realidade social brasileira.

O educador também participou de diversas reportagens da TV Bahia. Uma das participações mais recentes foi exibida em 13 de maio de 2026, em uma reportagem sobre a Conjuração Baiana.

Professor Bira Carlucio também se candidatou ao cargo de vereador pelo partido Partido Democrático Trabalhista (PDT). Ele recebeu 1.474 votos e ficou como suplente.

Em nota, a Fundação Gregório de Mattos (FGM) lamentou a morte do professor e destacou a contribuição dele para a educação patrimonial em Salvador.

Desde 2024, Bira participava do Circuito Reconectar, iniciativa da Prefeitura de Salvador voltada à valorização do patrimônio histórico e cultural da cidade.

No projeto, ele contribuiu para a formação de guias turísticos, professores e estudantes da rede municipal de ensino. O trabalho reunia conhecimentos de Geografia, História e patrimônio a partir de perspectivas decoloniais e antirracistas.

Em agosto deste ano, o professor também participou da 7ª Jornada do Patrimônio Cultural, com uma aula a bordo de uma escuna pela Baía de Todos-os-Santos.

O presidente da FGM, Fernando Guerreiro, destacou a generosidade do educador e o compromisso dele com a valorização da história. Já o diretor de Patrimônio Cultural da fundação, Vagner Rocha, ressaltou a contribuição de Bira para a educação patrimonial e para a construção de um olhar mais crítico sobre Salvador.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, a família não havia divulgado informações sobre o velório e o sepultamento.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro: entidades criticam fala sobre 'entraves ambientais' | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PL à Presidência fez afirmação durante ato de campanha em Marabá (PA). Entidades disseram que declaração reproduz o 'discurso mais atrasado' sobre Amazônia.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro é criticado por entidades ambientais após prometer o fim de entraves para produtores rurais fazerem o que quiserem em suas terras na Amazônia.
articles.body:
Entidades ambientalistas criticaram nesta terça-feira (20) uma declaração do senador Flávio Bolsonaro , candidato do PL à presidência da República, sobre acabar com o que chamou de "entraves ambientais" para permitir que produtores façam "o que quiserem" em suas terras.

Flávio fez a afirmação nesta segunda (19), ao participar de um ato de campanha com apoiadores em Marabá (PA). Ele cumpriu compromissos nos estados do Pará e do Amazonas, onde busca ampliar os votos em relação ao primeiro turno.

"Eu vou fazer a maior regularização fundiária que o Pará já viu e a sua terra vai ser sua pessoa no papel. Vamos respeitar a propriedade privada. Você vai poder plantar, criar gado, vai fazer o que quiser na sua terra, e o que você explorar da terra é seu. Esses entraves que existem, ambientais, e principalmente por causa de razões ideológicas, a gente vai acabar”, disse Flávio no evento.

Para o Instituto Socioambiental (ISA), Flávio Bolsonaro reproduziu "o discurso mais atrasado" sobre a Amazônia, tratando a região como uma área em que pode haver desmatamento para viabilizar o aumento da produção agropecuária.

“Desconsidera tudo que a ciência e a experiência dos povos e comunidades tradicionais já comprovaram. O valor da Amazônia está na floresta em pé e nos serviços ambientais que ela presta. No contexto das mudanças climáticas, a Amazônia é única no mundo e tratá-la como uma área qualquer a ser ocupada em um modelo predatório e de baixa inovação é voltar à década de 1970, conhecida como a década da destruição”, afirmou o ISA.

Na mesma linha, a coordenadora de Desmatamento Zero do Greenpeace Brasil, Cristiane Mazzetti, afirma que o meio ambiente não deve ser tratado como uma questão "ideológica" ou "oportunista", pois a preservação envolve toda a sociedade.

“Recentemente, celebramos a menor taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia desde o início da série histórica, em 1988. Estes bons resultados na queda do desmatamento vistos desde 2023 estão ameaçados pela eleição de um negacionista que vê o meio ambiente como ideologia”, afirmou Cristiane.

"Proteções ambientais não são 'entraves'. O que o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro vê como 'entrave' é, na prática, a garantia do direito ao meio ambiente ecologicamente equilibrado para as presentes e futuras gerações […] e a proteção contra danos irreversíveis ao clima, à biodiversidade e à natureza”, emendou.

Durante o governo de Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2023), pai de Flávio, se tornou pública uma frase dita pelo então ministro do Meio Ambiente, Ricardo Salles, durante uma reunião ministerial no Palácio do Planalto. Na ocasião, Salles sugeriu a Bolsonaro que adotasse medidas para passar a "boiada" na regulamentação ambiental .

Na ocasião, ele argumentou que era o momento de o então governo Bolsonaro adotar medidas que flexibilizassem as regras ambientais enquanto a atenção da população estava voltada ao noticiário sobre a pandemia da Covid-19.

Recordando essa declaração de Salles, o secretário-executivo do Observatório do Clima, Marcio Astrini, avaliou que a afirmação de Flávio Bolsonaro durante o ato de campanha nesta segunda-feira representa um "risco" de o Brasil retomar as ideias de Jair Bolsonaro no meio ambiente.

"É o risco de voltarmos aos tempos do governo Bolsonaro, os mais sombrios da história para a agenda ambiental, onde a proteção ao meio ambiente era tratada como inimiga e o desmatamento era política de governo”, declarou.

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) durante evento com apoiadores em Manaus na noite de segunda-feira (19). — Foto: Patrick Marques/g1 AM

articles.title: Meta diz ao TSE que tomou medidas para candidaturas serem tratadas de forma igual | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro do TSE determinou que empresa apresentasse comprovação de que atendeu às regras estabelecidas pela Justiça Eleitoral para garantir tratamento idêntico a candidaturas.
articles.summary: Ministro do TSE determinou que empresa apresentasse comprovação de que atendeu às regras estabelecidas pela Justiça Eleitoral para garantir tratamento idêntico a candidaturas.
articles.body:
A empresa Meta (dona do Facebook , WhatsApp e Instagram) respondeu ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) nesta terça-feira (20), e afirma que cumpriu as determinações da Corte para garantir isonomia na distribuição de conteúdos políticos e na veiculação de anúncios eleitorais durante o segundo turno das eleições.

No documento, a empresa diz que uma declaração técnica juntada ao processo "atesta que os conteúdos relativos às duas candidaturas são tratados de forma igual e não discriminatória, e descreve o mecanismo que assegura essa isonomia".

Além disso, também declara que não houve negligência nem resistência ao cumprimento das determinações do TSE (veja o que ficou estabelecido aqui).

"O Facebook Brasil e as equipes da Meta trabalham de forma incessante para produzir a documentação em cumprimento das dezessete alíneas da ordem", afirma o texto.

O documento foi enviado ao TSE após decisão do ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze . Ele determinou nessa segunda-feira (19) que a empresa apresentasse, em até 24 horas , um detalhamento das medidas tomadas para garantir igualdade entre as campanhas.

Manifestação em frente à sede da Meta em SP — Foto: TV Globo

Além do documento enviado ao TSE, a Meta também publicou um texto sobre o tema.

"Apesar de nossos melhores esforços, poderão ocorrer erros, incluindo o bloqueio indevido de anúncios de anunciantes autorizados – justamente o tipo de problema que deu origem a este processo judicial. Informamos isso ao TSE e trabalharemos rapidamente com o tribunal e com as equipes de campanha para corrigir quaisquer problemas", diz o texto.

E prossegue: "Essa determinação judicial também significa que entidades governamentais e outras organizações, incluindo ONGs, veículos de imprensa e grupos que veiculam anúncios sobre temas sociais, não poderão exibir esses anúncios no Brasil a partir de segunda-feira, 19 de outubro, até depois do segundo turno, em 25 de outubro".

"A determinação diz respeito apenas a anúncios e não afeta as publicações orgânicas nem as discussões sobre eleições, política e temas sociais em nossos aplicativos".

A decisão atendeu a um pedido da campanha do presidente Lula, candidato à reeleição. A ação enviada pela equipe do petista afirma que a Meta "tem falhado, de forma reiterada e sistemática, na entrega de postagens da coligação".

A campanha também mencionou que comandos para geração de imagens de inteligência artificial não permitem a criação de conteúdos sobre Lula. Ainda de acordo com a petição, a criação de imagens relacionadas ao candidato Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) está liberada.

Segundo a coligação, há indícios de tratamento desigual na distribuição de conteúdos políticos pela plataforma.

Os advogados da coligação afirmaram ainda que perfis ligados à candidatura adversária, entre eles o do deputado Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG), registrariam números de visualizações considerados incompatíveis com os parâmetros usuais da plataforma.

Cueva também determinou que a Meta (responsável pelo WhatsApp, Instagram e Facebook) e o X suspendam o impulsionamento pago de conteúdos publicados pelas contas de Nikolas e Marçal até o fim do segundo turno.

Em caso de descumprimento, a multa prevista é de R$ 50 mil por publicação. A decisão também vale para posts considerados reproduções substancialmente idênticas aos conteúdos vetados, mesmo que não sejam os mesmos.

As plataformas também não poderão conceder tratamento privilegiado a esses perfis na distribuição de propaganda eleitoral.

Em 15 de outubro, o ministro Marco Aurélio Bellizze determinou que a Meta:

não aplique a conteúdos políticos-eleitorais relativos a qualquer das candidaturas que disputam o segundo turno medidas de redução de distribuição, de exclusão de recomendação, ou de restrição de busca;

precisa, no prazo de 24 horas, limitar a exclusão dos sistemas de recomendação aos perfis oficiais; e

desabilite ou restrinja as contas de anúncios das candidaturas.

Ainda de acordo com a decisão, a empresa precisa assegurar que a Meta AI aplique critério idêntico às candidaturas.

articles.title: Vance Declines Netanyahu Endorsement as Trump Backs Bibi
articles.summary: Vance Declines Netanyahu Endorsement as Trump Backs Bibi
articles.body:
Vice President JD Vance declined Monday to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection, while President Donald Trump gave the embattled Israeli leader his "Complete and Total Endorsement" ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 election.

"I endorse American candidates ... so I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections," Vance said in an interview with journalist Mark Halperin, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Vance said he was neither supporting nor opposing Netanyahu, explaining that his focus was on the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.

Trump on Sunday praised Netanyahu as a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a partner in confronting Iran, adding that without Netanyahu in office, the United States might have to finish the fight against Tehran on its own.

Netanyahu thanked Trump for the backing, writing on X, "Together we will complete the mission!"

The endorsement came as Netanyahu seeks another term amid polls suggesting his governing coalition could fall short of a parliamentary majority. Israelis will vote in the country's first national election since Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack and the ensuing regional wars.

Vance's stance contrasts with his decision to campaign in Hungary in April for then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who lost his reelection bid.

Meanwhile, War Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday and met with Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, Axios reported, citing two sources familiar with the trip.

Reuters said it could not independently confirm the visit, and the Pentagon and Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately comment.

The visit came amid U.S.-Israeli discussions about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran, according to Axios.

articles.title: Trump approval at record-low 31 percent ahead of midterms: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating on Monday reached a new record low with two weeks left until the November midterm elections, where Republicans could lose the House and Senate to Democrats. The latest polling from Reuters/Ipsos shows the president with a 31 percent approval rating, down 1 point since the previous poll two weeks ago and…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating on Monday reached a new record low with two weeks left until the November midterm elections, where Republicans could lose the House and Senate to Democrats.

The latest polling from Reuters/Ipsos shows the president with a 31 percent approval rating, down 1 point since the previous poll two weeks ago and the lowest point in both of his terms. Sixty-six percent of respondents said they did not approve of his job performance.

Respondents disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy at 68 percent, including 37 percent of self-identified Republicans.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey is the latest of several polls showing Trump’s approval rating dipping lower and lower with two years left in his second term. Polling on Sunday from The Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos found the president with a 33 percent approval rating , 4 points lower than a poll conducted in July and lower than at any time during his first term.

The latest poll also asked respondents whom they would vote for if the election were held today, with 47 percent of registered voters favoring Democrats and 35 percent backing Republicans on a generic ballot. That also marked the widest margin in the Reuters/Ipsos poll this election cycle.

The same poll two weeks ago showed registered voters saying they preferred Democrats over Republicans to control Congress, at 44 percent and 37 percent, respectively.

Trump’s approval rating has plummeted in the months since he authorized strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. The ensuing conflict, unpopular with the American public, led to rising gas prices nationwide following Iran’s effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.

The president has sought to ease gas and diesel prices, but the price at the pump has stayed consistently high despite a slight dip in recent weeks. The average cost of gas in the U.S. hit $4.28 per gallon on Tuesday, almost $1.30 more than the average at this time last year, according to AAA .

Trump has called on voters to “ pretend I’m on the ballot ,” pledging to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if the GOP holds on to its control of both chambers of Congress. Stumping for Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in Kansas on Monday, Trump announced an $8 billion fund to offset diesel costs for farmers during the harvest season.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted Oct. 16-19 and included 1,679 respondents. The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

articles.title: The wheels are flying off the wagon
articles.summary: Between Oct. 11 and Oct. 18, 2026, President Trump faced widespread criticism following several controversial decisions, including the appointment of a press secretary, a proposal for televised executions, a modified Russia sanction deal, and the release of an AI-generated video involving a tiger.
articles.body:
Today, for regular or occasional readers of this column, and for those of you tuning in for the first time, I only have only one request. Before reading any further, please put your partisanship on hold.

Forget about politics for the moment and consider shocking cases of mismanagement we saw last week alone from the Trump White House between Oct. 11 and Oct. 18. The facts do not lie.

First, President Trump himself named Katie Zacharia the new White House press secretary. She gave one disastrous 15-minute press briefing. She lasted all of five days. Trump has no one to blame but himself.

Unlike other potential candidates, during the two months since former press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she was stepping down, Zacharia was never interviewed or vetted for the job. She called herself a lawyer , which she’s not. She flunked her bar exam . She also had no prior journalism experience, other than occasional appearances on Fox News. For Trump, that was enough to give her the job — reportedly over the objections of chief of staff Susie Wiles. One major self-inflicted embarrassment.

Second, reportedly over the objections of top staffers, Trump announced his support for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to publicly televise the firing squad execution of 2009 Fort Hood shooter and former U.S. Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan. It would be, he wrote on Truth Social , “a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.” It would also, Trump did not add, put the United States in the company of Iran and Afghanistan, the only other countries which carried out public executions in 2025.

The response to Trump’s announcement was immediate and fierce. Both Republicans and Democrats in Congress condemned the plan. Eighty percent of Americans expressed their opposition.

The archbishop who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to Catholics in the U.S. military urged Catholics not to take part in the firing squad . Vice President JD Vance said he wouldn’t watch it.

A few days later, stung by the backlash, Trump cancelled the livestream, but not before handing himself a third self-inflicted wound. On Sept. 18, in an elaborate Oval Office ceremony, he had signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, imposing new sanctions and tariffs on Russia for its continued war against Ukraine. Trump hailed the act, which passed the House in a lopsided, bipartisan 262-159 vote , as a posthumous tribute to Graham, his No. 1 supporter in the Senate.

Yet on Oct. 16, two days before the new sanctions were to take effect, Trump signed an executive order taking all teeth out of them, making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to sell diesel fuel to the U.S.

Again, the backlash was furious. Republican senators accused Trump of betraying them and Graham. Critics pointed out that Trump was providing Putin with funding to continue his war against Ukraine — a war, remember, Trump promised to end on Day One. Moreover, the first installment of Trump’s Putin deal would only provide Americans with less than half a day of average diesel consumption. All three installments in the Trump-Putin agreement would provide Americans with less than two weeks of fuel . It was a rotten deal and another big embarrassment.

Fourth, and perhaps most bizarrely, hours after posting video of a mentally ill man climbing into a tiger enclosure in an English zoo and getting mauled to death, Trump released an AI-generated video of himself wrestling with a tiger and, of course, tackling it into submission.

The victim’s British family accused Trump of cruelty by publicly releasing video of their son’s gruesome death, while Americans were left scratching their head over what message Trump was trying to send by posting fake videos.

Now, I remind you: These are only shocking actions taken by Trump between Oct. 11 and Oct. 18. This isn’t about his waging a pointless, ongoing war with Iran, trying to kick reporters whose stories he doesn’t like out of the White House, tearing down the East Wing of the White House, shutting down the Kennedy Center, and running illegal, self-promotional television ads paid for by taxpayers.

Again, putting any partisanship aside, you must admit: Trump is out of control. If any CEO ran his company like this, he’d be fired before he could open his golden parachute.

articles.title: The Movement: Paris is burning. The American right is watching.
articles.summary: Protests and riots in France have become the latest Republican talking point in the U.S. as the party makes a last-ditch effort to tie Democrats to immigration and socialism two weeks out from the midterm elections. Protesters, largely high school students, first took to the streets earlier this month to demand better school conditions. Those…
articles.body:
Protests and riots in France have become the latest Republican talking point in the U.S. as the party makes a last-ditch effort to tie Democrats to immigration and socialism two weeks out from the midterm elections.

Protesters, largely high school students, first took to the streets earlier this month to demand better school conditions. Those demonstrations turned into wider protests on cost-of-living issues in the country, which have descended into riots and looting in major French cities.

Saturday saw the largest outbreak of protests so far — with about 2,400 people arrested nationally.

The unrest has put a sharp focus on French political tensions ahead of its elections next year. But Republicans have seized on the imagery as a warning to voters of the social and political chaos Democrats would sow if they clinch power on Nov. 3.

“France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America,” Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) wrote in a post on social media. “What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.”

Both President Trump and Vice President Vance also sought to link the situation in France to Democrats , particularly immigration policy.

“The migrants have taken over France,” Trump wrote Monday morning on Truth Social. “They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!”

Vance wrote on social media over the weekend that, “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion.”

“I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn,” he continued. ”And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.”

The photos and video of the unrest in France are red meat for the GOP base. Republicans have long pointed to immigration policy and unrest in Western Europe as a cautionary tale in their push for more restrictive border policy in the U.S.

Ongoing protests in France have focused on education and the economy, not immigration. French officials have not suggested there is any link between immigration and the protest activity.

“What you’re seeing in France is the natural and eventual consequence of the Suicidal Empathy so many in The West have adopted,” Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) wrote on social media . “It’s one of the reasons I fight so hard on the mass migration issue here in our homeland — America. It’s not too late but we must take illegal immigration, problems with legal immigration seriously and not flinch on deportations.”

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) used similar language , alluding to the region’s growing Muslim population.

“We are witnessing Islamists right now burning Paris because Europe has committed cultural suicide,” Cruz said. “We should look to France as foreshadowing for what America faces if we don’t stop this here. We are fighting to save our nation.”

Kevin Roberts , president of the Heritage Foundation, also suggested the protesters were immigrants or otherwise not native French, in a social post responding to French President Emmanuel Macron’s call for peace over the weekend.

“Mr. Macron, the people you are fecklessly asking to stop burning down your country hardly understand the language you speak, nor do they care,” Roberts wrote . “There are lessons you refuse to learn, and so France will continue to burn.”

Republicans are also taking any chance they get to tie Democrats to socialism, antisemitism and general urban mayhem as their own political disadvantage grows more pronounced in the lead-up to the election.

Socialism in particular has been a key talking point for Republicans, who point to historic wins by democratic socialist candidates in primary elections this year.

“This is what happens when leaders lose the will to defend their country and the rule of law. America must never follow this path,” Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) wrote on social media .

“We have a civilization worth defending, and we’d better have the courage to defend it against bad DSA ideas that are anti-police, anti-law enforcement, anti-capitalist, and anti-American. This could be our future if these ideas prevail,” he added, referencing the Democratic Socialists of America.

Conservatives were also quick to look for evidence of a conspiracy from left-wing groups riling up protesters or otherwise provoking violence. There were other anti-government protests over the weekend in other European cities, including Lisbon and Milan .

Andrew Kolvet, spokesperson for Turning Point USA, suggested the France protests were part of a larger scheme from the far left. He referred to a report from Fox News Digital alleging that 54 organizations, including labor unions, left-leaning political groups and human rights organizations “helped organize and amplify” the original student protests.

“You still think it’s a bunch of students in France and now Milan? Well the same socialist and communist groups behind those riots are planning a November 20th ‘demonstration’ spanning 12 countries,” Kolvet wrote. “It’s all funded and coordinated.”

The response from some on the left has not assuaged those concerns on the right.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) , one of the most vocal economic progressives in Congress, suggested that the protests shed light on people’s dissatisfaction with wealth inequality.

“From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in,” Khanna wrote on social media.

“[This] is what happens when nations let wealth and power accumulate in the hands of a few. This is what happens when young people lose hope in their future. In America, let us listen to our young.”

After garnering criticism, Khanna clarified that he condemned the violence and vandalism.

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

How conservative groups have spent midterm cash

PACs pour millions into battleground Senate contests

Elon Musk’s America PAC donated $158 million in the last quarter to Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), associated with Senate Republicans. The SLF immediately put that money into the Texas Senate race to back embattled GOP nominee Ken Paxton .

Musk’s group has already spent big for Republicans elsewhere. He invested more than $76 million for Senate candidates in Michigan and Alaska as well as a host of House races.

The Republican National Committee is now wading in, too, with an unprecedented $4 million ad spend coordinated with the campaign to help Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) win Iowa’s open seat. And the National Republican Senatorial Committee is launching coordinated spends too, with $614,000 to support Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall (R) , according to AdImpact.

Meanwhile, a new super PAC linked to national Republicans jumped into the Nebraska Senate race last week with $1.4 million, backing Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) .

Heavy hitters move money as races slide off map

National Republicans already shifted funds out of North Carolina’s Senate race — which is looking increasingly favorable for Democrats — to toss-up Kansas.

Democrats and Republicans have also slowed their spending in Georgia’s Senate race as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) becomes increasingly likely to keep his seat.

Republicans are almost certain to move more money around as they play defense on Senate seats in Alaska, Ohio and Iowa. MAGA Inc., the super PAC affiliated with Trump, is expected to pull out of several House races to instead put more money behind the Senate majority, according to Politico.

The GOP will also send millions to seats it could still flip. The Michigan Senate race is one of the most expensive in the country by ad spending. Republicans have $28.6 million in ad spending reserved there so far, against Democrats’ $11.3 million, according to AdImpact .

As Trump’s approval rating continues to sink, Republican candidates and strategists are adjusting the content of their programming. GOP ads mention Trump less and less, according to an analysis from AdImpact .

Republican candidates in the toughest races are also speaking out more against Trump policies, including the war on Iran and the tariffs with Canada .

Insead, groups and candidates are looking to validate voters’ concerns about the economy while encouraging them not to vote for Democrats. Americans for Prosperity Action, an organization aligned with the Koch family, launched a new series of ads last week in five states featuring actors speaking directly to the camera, complaining about high prices but deciding that socialism — and by extension, the Democratic candidate — “is not the answer.”

Anti-abortion groups demand CDC better monitor incidence

Several anti-abortion groups are calling on the Trump administration to establish new reporting requirements for maternal mortality and abortion incidence. The groups wrote in a letter published Wednesday that abortions are undercounted in Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) statistics and suggested policy moves to fix this.

“We appreciate your commitment to data integrity and transparency and for acknowledging that abortion surveillance is ‘an absolutely critical component of what the CDC is currently doing’ alongside the agency’s surveillance of maternal mortality,” the letter addressed to new CDC Director Erica Schwartz said. “We believe women should be provided with excellent healthcare, starting with accurate public health information.”

The organizations that signed the letter include Americans United for Life, Christian Medical and Dental Associations, the American Association of Pro-Life OBGYNs and the Catholic Medical Association.

The specific concern, the letter details, is that statistics about maternal mortality rates per year are calculated against the number of live births, rather than all pregnancy outcomes (including abortions). Including this statistic would create a more thorough picture of how abortions affect maternal mortality outcomes, the groups argue.

“Fixing broken maternal mortality and abortion reporting measures is the stopgap slowing breakthroughs in women’s healthcare,” said Gavin Oxley , spokesperson for Americans United for Life. “Women and their healthcare providers should be equipped with the highest quality data to inform their pregnancy decisions, saving lives. Reforms at the CDC should be embraced with bipartisan support.”

Schwartz, in her July confirmation hearing, signaled openness to further monitoring the incidence of abortions in the U.S.

Republicans of all stripes are pushing back on Trump’s move to undercut the bipartisan Russia sanctions bill. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said Monday he warned the White House about consequences of loosening Russian sanctions, and several Republican senators also fired off critical social media posts over the weekend. The Wall Street Journal Editorial Board also had harsh words for Trump’s renewed warmth toward Moscow.

Some conservative groups are trying to determine whether Trump’s latest pick for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit is conservative enough. G. Todd Butler , the judge, has a quiet record on political issues he may have to deal with on the New Orleans-based appellate court. More here.

Older Republicans’ entrenched negative views of certain countries, especially China, Russia, Canada and Mexico, are somewhat lost on their younger counterparts. Republicans and Republican-leaning independents aged 18-34 viewed Russia and China nearly 10 points more favorably than Republicans aged 50 and over in a recent Pew Research Center survey .

articles.title: Manchin: Matthew McConaughey ‘absolutely so accurate’ on independents
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Monday said actor Matthew McConaughey was “absolutely so accurate” in his premidterm election message calling on Americans to choose independent candidates who will help bring Congress back to the political center. “He is absolutely so accurate,” Manchin told “The Hill” host Blake Burman on NewsNation. “It’s not that [you]…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) on Monday said actor Matthew McConaughey was “absolutely so accurate” in his premidterm election message calling on Americans to choose independent candidates who will help bring Congress back to the political center.

“He is absolutely so accurate,” Manchin told “The Hill” host Blake Burman on NewsNation. “It’s not that [you] run through them. It means you have to run with them. If they don’t go with you and you’re completely extreme to the left or to the right, you can’t get anywhere.”

McConaughey referred to Manchin’s organization that launched last year , the Independent Leadership Council, in his social media post on Sunday, calling for a “fair fight” in the midterms, saying the U.S.’s “No. 1 identity … is independent.”

“So independents belong in the fight — not as a protest, not as a spoiler — but as a real and potential winner, on the ballot and considered seriously by us,” the actor said in a post on the social platform X .

McConaughey said Manchin knew “the math” and “took all the fire” for being an independent in the Senate.

Manchin echoed the actor’s sentiments in his interview with Burman on Monday.

“If you want to get something done and you have two, three, or four in the middle [who] says, ‘I will work with either side who has our country’s best interest at heart,’ that’s where we’ll go,” he continued. “And you can count on us being there, but not any other way. If you’re playing just to the party to demonize the other side, count us out. We’re out of this. We don’t belong to either one of you. This is what the country started. This is how it was intended to be.”

The former Democratic senator said the message harkened back to President George Washington’s farewell address warning against political factions, “for they can become the engines that usurp the power from the people.”

“The power of the parties gets so powerful, Blake,” Manchin continued. “How do they control everything? How do they get all the elections to where they’re able to control –– change the laws and change the rules?”

If Democrats win back power in Congress, he urged his former party to restore a balance of power but “hit the ground running” to tackle the cost of living, lower the national debt and “get people’s lives in a better position.”

“If you’re going for retaliation and retribution, you’re going down the primrose path you can’t return from,” he said.

As for a possible future in politics for the “True Detective” actor, Manchin said McConaughey “has the ability” to one day run for president.

“He’s smart. He’s charismatic,” Manchin said. “He’s able to communicate. He’s able to tell a story that makes sense and you’ll listen to. He has all the qualities and all the ingredients that it takes to bring this country together. Now, if that’s where he wishes to go or whatever, I’d be 1,000 percent behind him. Absolutely.”

Two independents –– Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), a progressive, and Angus King (I-Maine), a moderate –– serve in the Senate, while Rep. Kevin Kiley (I-Calif.), formerly a Republican, is facing a tough race for reelection as the only unaffiliated House member.

articles.title: Kimberly Guilfoyle’s sacking drains a drop from Trump’s overflowing swamp
articles.summary: Guilfoyle is small potatoes.
articles.body:
Trump’s newly minted press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was fired almost before she was hired.

In her maiden appearance last week, Zacharia, who had claimed to be a lawyer but never passed the bar, nervously read off a terse script about Donald Trump Jr’s ex-fiancée Kimberly Guilfoyle, who recently stepped down as ambassador to Greece, calling her “a wonderful asset to the team,” and saying they “wish her well.”

Zacharia was not a deft communicator. In fact, Guilfoyle was forced to resign over improprieties. Andy Borowitz chortled over the news with a satirical Trump Jr. saying: “When Kimberly and I were together, I worried that we didn’t have enough in common. But now that I see that she was using her proximity to power for financial gain, I realize I was very wrong.”

Corruption, conflict of interest and influence peddling are nothing new in the Trump administration, and so few were surprised when Guilfoyle was recalled. She was forced out following a string of damaging reports, including that she had asked a Trump donor to pay her $100,000 American Express bill.

The donor, Eric Deters, told The Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle asked him to wire her the funds just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. She wanted the funds transferred in a way that wouldn’t leave a paper trail.

“Honey, please,” she pleaded . Deters declined, saying , “Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work. I can’t do this without getting a divorce.”

According to messages Deters provided to The New York Times , Guilfoyle promised to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he sent her the money. “Every secretary you know defense, transportation, treasury commerce IRS commissioner everyone gets right back to me,” she wrote Deters, shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.

But Guilfoyle is small potatoes. Last year, Trump raked in over $2 billion , more than half of which came from crypto even as his administration gutted the primary regulator of the industry . Trump’s sons stand to reap a fortune from a billion-dollar tungsten mining venture in Kazakhstan. The joint venture is set to receive up to $1.6 billion in federal financing.

Trump Jr. is a consultant to a company called GrabAGun and a member of its board. GrabAGun sells and ships ammunition and some gun accessories directly to consumers through its website. The administration has proposed regulatory changes that would let firearms sales take place entirely online, with handguns mailed directly to buyers’ doorsteps. If they go through, Trump Jr. stands to make millions.

A White House official has said the new proposed rules were driven by Second Amendment interests and had nothing to do with Trump Jr.’s business ventures. Really? And as spice in the stew, there was Trump, Jr.’s lavish wedding on two private islands funded by a Putin allied oligarch .

Trump said Tuesday that Guilfoyle “was doing a good job” but that he “didn’t like what I read.” He also downplayed his connection to Guilfoyle, who, as noted, was once engaged to his son.

Guilfoyle has a past. In 2018 , she started dating Trump Jr. and working for a pro-Trump super PAC . The two were engaged in 2020 , and Guilfoyle spoke at both the 2020 and 2024 Republican National Conventions. In May, Trump Jr. married Bettina Anderson , a Palm Beach socialite.

Guilfoyle got around politically. Her four-year marriage to now-California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) ended in divorce in 2006. In 2004, Harper’s Bazaar predicted their marriage would be “one of the most glamorous political unions since Jack and Jackie.” How the mighty have fallen.

In a lengthy post on social media, Guilfoyle said that she planned to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

Guilfoyle was one of the first ambassadors nominated in Trump’s second term. In Greece, she has been highly visible, appearing on the cover of Vogue Greece and at parties around Athens. She told The Times last year that her active social life evinced her commitment to the job.

And here’s another one, tucked in between the social and business pages, a Turkish businessman, 29-year-old investor Turhan Mildon, once allied with the Maduro regime in Venezuela, tied the knot in a lavish New York ceremony last month. He married Trump’s former personal lawyer, Alina Habba, 42. The groom is seeking to preserve a big Venezuelan cement contract.

It was a stunning Trumpworld debut for Mildon, who nearly a year ago faced the loss of his extensive business interests in Venezuela because of his ties to the inner circle of Maduro, the Venezuelan leader captured by U.S. commandos in January.

Mildon explained his business strategy to Forbes Turkey as follows: “In my grandfather’s time, know-how, was very important,” Mildon told the magazine. “Now, know-who is important.”

White House officials said that Habba has not discussed her husband’s business dealings with Trump or any other White House officials. Tell me another one. She has maintained a close relationship with Trump and visited him in the Oval Office in recent weeks.

Americans care about corruption. The issue may well be the Democrat’s horse to ride back into town.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: When return-to-office mandates cause a family crisis
articles.summary: For fathers, working from home affects family routines, caregiving, mothers’ careers, mental health, retention and the silent career tax attached to visible care.
articles.body:
The fight over return-to-office mandates keeps getting framed as a management question: How many days should employees be present in the building?

A new report from King’s College London, by Shiyu Yuan and Professor Heejung Chung, shows why that frame misses the point. For fathers, working from home affects family routines, caregiving, mothers’ careers, mental health, retention and the silent career tax attached to visible care.

The central finding deserves more executive attention. Yuan and Chung report that full-time fathers in the United Kingdom want about twice as many homeworking days as employers allow — around 2.10 preferred days compared with 1.10 allowed days. They also find that fathers’ stated willingness to quit outright if forced back to the office full time had risen to about 17 percent by June 2025, up from about 5 percent in early 2022.

That should unsettle leaders who treat office attendance as a low-risk cultural reset.

The broader labor market supports the same conclusion. The Office for National Statistics found that working parents were more likely to hybrid work than non-parents in Great Britain, and male working parents were more likely to hybrid work than female working parents. That does not mean every parent wants the same arrangement; it means fathers are already using hybrid work as part of household infrastructure.

The old breadwinner model no longer explains most professional families. Pew Research Center findings summarized by The Associated Press show that dual full-time working parents now make up 52 percent of different-sex couples with children under 18, up from 31 percent in 1975. When both parents work full time, flexibility becomes less like a perk and more like plumbing — nobody praises plumbing until it breaks.

Yuan and Chung also make a sharper equality argument. Fathers working from home can help rebalance child care and housework, but the benefit depends on whether men can use flexibility without stigma. In UK households surveyed during COVID lockdowns, fathers who worked from home were three times more likely to increase their share of child care than fathers who did not. Their report also cites evidence that when only the father worked from home and the mother held a higher occupational position, the mother’s share of housework fell from 67 percent to 55 percent.

That matters, because unpaid work remains uneven. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that, on an average day in 2025, women spent more time on household activities than men, and women living with children under the age of six spent an hour more per day than men on primary child care. If companies pull fathers away from home without a clear business reason, they may push more unpaid labor back toward mothers.

What’s more, a working paper on men’s remote work and women’s labor supply found that increases in men’s work-from-home exposure improved wives’ labor-market outcomes, including employment, earnings, hours and weeks worked. The mechanism appears practical rather than symbolic: men at home covered more child-caring time, giving women more capacity for paid work.

Unfortunately, Yuan and Chung report that fathers who work from home face especially strong career penalties, particularly when they work from home three or four days a week. Managers often read physical presence as commitment and caregiving flexibility as reduced ambition. That creates remote work stigma even when output stays strong. Fathers then face a bad bargain: use flexibility and risk advancement, or hide caregiving and leave more strain at home.

Policy framing can reduce that penalty. Employees have a legal right to request flexible working from the first day in a job, including changes to where they work. Yet a right to request still places heavy weight on manager discretion. Employers are urged to consider requests reasonably, but organizations also need internal promotion data to see whether flexibility users pay a hidden price.

The business risk has already begun showing up in turnover. A study using 260 million resumes found that a large-company office mandate can shift tenure and seniority downward as experienced employees leave. Fathers are one visible part of a wider problem: rigid attendance policies can drain precisely the workers with judgment, continuity and family responsibilities that make them expensive to replace.

Leaders should stop asking whether fathers deserve special treatment, and ask instead whether their operating model punishes the people holding modern families together. Set anchor days for collaboration. Protect home days for focus and family logistics. Evaluate outcomes, not hallway sightings. Track promotions, raises and key assignments by work pattern, gender and parental status. Train managers to treat care-compatible work as normal work.

When fathers can work from home without penalty, employers gain retention, mothers gain room to sustain careers, and families gain practical capacity. When fathers cannot use flexibility safely, companies send a blunt message: care belongs somewhere else. That message no longer fits the workforce.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: Trump country at a crossroads
articles.summary: Rural voters are wavering on the GOP as cost of living, unemployment and AI data centers reshape the political landscape in heartland states.
articles.body: Republicans have had their share of good and bad election nights this century, but they’ve usually been able to count on the heartland. Once evenly divided, rural voters have become substantially more Republican over the last two decades. Nearly two-thirds of these voters backed President Trump in the 2024 election. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. Today, just under half of rural voters say they’ll support the GOP again in November. Like other groups, rural Americans are concerned about paying the bills. Nineteen percent said the rising cost of living is their biggest economic problem in a recent survey, with gas and energy costs not far behind. The Trump administration has, in part, tried to counter those anxieties by talking about job growth and the AI boom, but rural voters are frustrated about those issues too. Less than a quarter of rural voters say the economy is in good shape, and unemployment is a focal point: 8% called a lack of jobs and unemployment their biggest economic issue, and only 28% thought there were good or excellent job opportunities in their communities. DAVID MARCUS: ON THE GROUND IN MIDDLE AMERICA, FOUR ISSUES WILL DECIDE THE SENATE, AND NONE ARE AFFORDABILITY Data centers are part of the story too. Only 2% called it their biggest economic problem, but that number is larger than it seems. For 1 in 50 rural voters, data centers are a bigger problem than housing, the cost of living, or getting a job. These factors have put the Republicans in a tough spot all over the map. They are a reason why heartland states like Ohio and Iowa have been competitive most of the year and why more rural districts, including some that Trump won by double digits, are becoming margin-of-error races. Even setting the polls aside, there are signs that the rural vote is on shakier footing. TV viewers in Wyoming will see ads this week for Republican candidate Chuck Gray that don’t mention Trump or the GOP. Two years ago, Trump won 71.6% of the vote there — his best performance in any state, in any election. Low rural turnout or party switching would make many races closer than the GOP would like, including in Florida, Mississippi and South Carolina. Four states are worth singling out thanks to another complicating factor. TRUMP-ALIGNED CONSERVATIVE EMERGES FROM CROWDED PRIMARY TO DECIDE WHO FILLS WYOMING’S LONE HOUSE SEAT This year, prominent independent candidates are running for Senate against a Republican in four rural-heavy states: Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota. They are pushing anti-establishment policies like congressional term limits and lobbying bans and have a heavy focus on corruption, the top voter concern in last week’s Fox News poll. And all four say they won’t caucus with either party or would form their own independent caucus if they were elected. With the Democratic brand still relatively weak around the country and abysmal in these states, the party has stepped out of the race entirely in three of the four (in Montana, a Democrat is staying on the ballot, though support for her has declined). Normally, frustrated partisans stay home in scenarios like these, leaving the incumbent party to win by a more modest margin. This year, those voters have the ability to turn out for a different candidate, so the margin may get narrower. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY All these states have been competitive over the last decade or so. Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Democrat, held on to his seat in Montana in 2018; Republicans have scored single-digit victories in South Dakota and Nebraska (where the same independent is running again this year), and even Idaho had a gubernatorial race that came within 15 points back in 2014. These states could be close again. In this week’s Power Rankings, two gubernatorial races get more competitive as the final two weeks of campaigning begin. Florida The Sunshine State is the beating heart of the "MAGA" movement. Trump and Gov. Ron DeSantis have posted stronger results each time they’ve run, with the latter winning his last re-election bid by nearly 20 points. Thanks in part to those performances, Republicans have carved out structural advantages, including a 1.5 million registered voter gap and a resilient get-out-the-vote operation. But DeSantis’ first win came within around 30,000 votes (or 0.4 points) and in a similar environment to the one we’re in now. Here, Hispanic voters will play an outsized role, and polls suggest that a large chunk of them have shifted away from the GOP. In last week’s national Fox survey, 31% of Hispanic voters said they preferred the Republican candidate over the Democrat. That’s down 12 points from their support for Trump in 2024. The Republican candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds, will be pleased to have the endorsement of DeSantis. He remains popular in the state. Donalds still has the edge against Democrat and former Rep. David Jolly, who is hoping former President Bill Clinton can shore up his support when they appear together for the first time today. Still, this race is no sure thing for the GOP. Florida moves from Likely R to Lean R. Nebraska In Nebraska, Republican Gov. Jim Pillen is looking for a second term in office. He cruised to victory the first time with a 23-point win, but with both suburban and rural voters wavering on Trump this cycle, this could be a tougher battle. Three other factors are playing a role. First, the presence of Dan Osborn, one of the four notable independents on the ballot in Senate races this year, could boost Democratic turnout for challenger Lynne Walz in a governor’s race that would otherwise attract less attention. There’s Pillen himself, who has faced some local pushback over a 5% budget cut and hiring freeze within state government. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Finally, the ballot, which will feature third-party challenger Brett Lindstrom, a former state lawmaker who lost to Pillen in a Republican primary four years prior. He’ll appear on the ballot as an "America First" candidate. The party was founded in July.

articles.body:
President Trump’s envoys will hold meetings Tuesday in Norway with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, along with the leaders of Norway and Finland, the Norwegian government said, as Trump pushes for an end to Russia and Ukraine’s nearly five-year conflict.

Trump on Monday told reporters, “All I want for Russia and Ukraine is for them to stop the stupid war.” Steve Witkoff will meet with Zelensky and others in person, with Jared Kushner meeting virtually.

Trump and Vice President Vance on Tuesday are set to make an announcement on a whistleblower “incentive program” from the Oval Office at 1:30 p.m. EDT.

“Every day, President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars and giving Americans the accountability they deserve. This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said.

With just two weeks before November’s midterms, Trump will continue his GOP midterm tour later in the day, travelling to Greenville, N.C., for a rally.

He is expected to make a case for Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, but polls place his Democratic opponent Gov. Roy Cooper firmly in the lead . The president also hosted a rally last month in Gastonia, N.C.

articles.title: O’Reilly: Trump ‘looks at Putin in a different way’
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday weighed in on President Trump’s recent decision to loosen sanctions on Russia. When asked by NewsNation’s Leland Vittert about how his perspective differs from the president’s on Russian President Vladimir Putin, O’Reilly said Trump “looks at Putin in a different way.” The former Fox News host pointed to his…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday weighed in on President Trump’s recent decision to loosen sanctions on Russia.

When asked by NewsNation’s Leland Vittert about how his perspective differs from the president’s on Russian President Vladimir Putin, O’Reilly said Trump “looks at Putin in a different way.”

The former Fox News host pointed to his 2017 interview with Trump in which O’Reilly said, “Putin’s a killer,” and the president replied, “There are a lot of killers.”

“So Trump is going to deal with you even if you’re a killer,” O’Reilly told Vittert. “He deals with Xi in China, and China commits all kinds of human rights violations.”

The commentator added that Trump “doesn’t have a line” like some of his predecessors.

In the past several weeks, the Trump administration lifted sanctions on Russian diesel and waived sanctions on the country days before they were set to be imposed under a newly signed sanctions package .

These moves drew bipartisan criticism from members of Congress, as well as pushback from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whose country has been engaged in a years-long war with Russia.

On Tuesday morning, Zelensky said he spoke with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and had a “substantive conversation” about ballistic missile interceptors, early warnings for Russian attacks and Starlink satellite access .

Rubio told reporters following the call there was “nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine.”

“It’s simply a balance between our obligations to other partners, and frankly, our own standards and requirements for our own facilities as well,” he continued.

A day before, Trump signaled he was open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. His comment followed reporting from The Wall Street Journal that Putin had proposed a trilateral meeting with China to discuss the war in Ukraine.

Trump told reporters Monday that he would not want to discuss Ukraine as much “because Russia, frankly, has been doing fine on Ukraine.”

Instead, the president said he wanted the meeting’s focus to center on “weapons and denuclearization.”

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned the meeting plans in a statement shared on social media and called for Ukraine to be included in the talks.

“A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S. and Russia could help end the war sooner,” he wrote. “A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war.”

articles.title: Acton’s estranged mother calls her a ‘liar’; Democrat calls Ramaswamy ‘despicable’
articles.summary: Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s (D) mother called her a “liar” in a new ad, as her brother labelled the video “a despicable low” on Tuesday ahead of the state’s elections in November. “I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent — it is not easy for a mother to…
articles.body:
Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton’s (D) mother called her a “liar” in a new ad, as her brother labelled the video “a despicable low” on Tuesday ahead of the state’s elections in November.

“I love my daughter, but when I saw her lying about her opponent — it is not easy for a mother to say this, but Amy has a serious problem. She is a liar,” Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, appeared to say in the ad .

“She lies about her past. She says she grew up living in a tent. None of that is true. She’s lied her entire life. My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself,” Arthur continued.

“People can change, but first they have to tell the truth. And my daughter still isn’t doing that. Don’t vote for people who lie. Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself. It will only get worse,” she concluded.

The ad appears to be a campaign-style video, but it is unclear who is backing or paying for it.

Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, responded in a press release to the ad on Tuesday, stating it was “not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.”

“After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died,” Stearns added.

Acton described her childhood following her parent’s divorce in detail during a 2019 interview with The Vindicator , remarking that while living with her mother she experienced abuse, neglect and a period of homelessness.

Eventually, charges were filed against Acton’s stepfather, and she moved in with her father and relatives.

Acton said in the 2019 interview the last time she spoke with her mother was in the courthouse where her stepfather was arrested, saying she “went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her.”

Acton is competing against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and is narrowly favored to flip the Ohio gubernatorial seat even though President Trump won the state in each of his presidential bids, according to The Hill’s partner, Decision Desk HQ.

Neither Acton’s nor Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Tillis: ‘Putin is playing President Trump like a fiddle’
articles.summary: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Russian President Vladimir Putin is playing President Trump “like a fiddle” by shifting U.S. support away from Ukraine and warned that “history” won’t judge Trump well if he abandons Ukraine. Tillis said Putin’s claim that he invaded Ukraine to “de-Nazify” the country is a lie and that Trump’s dealings with…
articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Russian President Vladimir Putin is playing President Trump “like a fiddle” by shifting U.S. support away from Ukraine and warned that “history” won’t judge Trump well if he abandons Ukraine.

Tillis said Putin’s claim that he invaded Ukraine to “de-Nazify” the country is a lie and that Trump’s dealings with Russia to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel and waive sanctions are a mistake that the U.S. will come to regret.

“Russians are lying. Putin is lying. Putin is playing President Trump like a fiddle. And history is not going to look good on an America that failed to rise up and defend the Western world if Putin actually gets his way,” Tillis told CNN in a Monday interview.

And Tillis slammed Putin’s proposed trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump as “absurd.”

“I believe that a summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, two countries who want to overwhelm the world, is absurd,” he said.

Tillis also questioned whether the Trump administration might be restricting military aid to Ukraine, despite official denials that it’s doing so.

“I want to know how the service has degraded over time — either intelligence sharing or the capabilities of Starlink,” Tillis said of reports last week that Ukraine had lost full access to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, and to critical U.S. intelligence.

Tillis and three other Republicans, including Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Susan Collins (Maine) and Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), signed a letter last week calling on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate whether any senior Pentagon officials ordered or had advance knowledge of a decision to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield and U.S. intelligence.

Tillis and several GOP senators have also denounced Trump’s deal to import several million tons of Russian diesel, which they warned would undercut U.S. credibility with allies and do little to reduce domestic fuel prices.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Tillis and other senators during a call Monday that Ukraine’s data speeds on Starshield had not been fully restored .

Zelensky also told lawmakers that it’s becoming more difficult for Ukraine to acquire Patriot missile interceptors to defend itself from Russian attacks.

“President Zelensky also mentioned that a part of what they want are simply Patriot missiles that are coming from third-party countries that are prepared to provide it” with approval from U.S. defense officials, Tillis told CNN.

“I want to know who in the government is saying no to those transfers. This is not even taking it from our inventories,” he said of the Patriot missiles that Zelensky claims are being withheld from Ukraine.

Trump’s handling of the Ukraine war and negotiations with Putin have drawn criticism from other conservative-leaning sources.

The Wall Street Journal published an editorial on Sunday declaring that “Mr. Trump is now Mr. Putin’s best friend in the world, after perhaps China’s Xi Jinping.”

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) posted the editorial on X , the social media platform, and commented that “Reagan and Lindsey would be ashamed of this,” referring to former President Reagan and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who sponsored a tough Russia sanctions package that Congress passed last month.

Trump on Friday waived the new law’s sanctions on Putin’s regime and its allies.

articles.title: Torched cars, ransacked businesses: Anti-Sharia crusader warns France 'civil war' could be imported to US
articles.summary: A top House Republican blames France riots on mass migration, warning America could face the same future if it doesn't learn from the Paris chaos.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: The top House Republican overseeing Europe policy is blaming the riots roiling French cities on mass migration, and warning the U.S. could soon follow suit. Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital that he was not surprised by the violent demonstrations across France — and moreover, argued they were a long time coming. "They've been allowing this to happen for years and years, so they are reaping what they sowed," Self said. "We're also trying to get a handle on our mass migration consequences, just like France should have done years ago. That's why I say this is a lesson to America. We are watching the future of America in France and the U.K., frankly." Self is the chairman of the Subcommittee on Europe in the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He is also a co-founder alongside Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, of the Sharia-Free America Caucus. VIOLENT FAR-LEFT RIOTS IN FRANCE ARE 'CHILLING WARNING' FOR AMERICANS AT HOME, MIKE JOHNSON SAYS Democrats have criticized the group as Islamophobic, and it's been condemned by groups like the U.S. Council of Muslim Organizations. But Self doubled down on his beliefs, suggesting France's growing Muslim population is at least partially responsible for the riots. "They've got, what, 7% now are Muslims in France? And, you know, when you reach that percentage — and very concentrated in some large cities — that gives you the tipping point that everybody talks about," he argued. Islam is the second-most popular religion in metropolitan France among people aged 18 to 59 after Catholicism, according to the country's National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. ITALY’S SCHOOL VEIL BAN EXPOSES EUROPE’S ASSIMILATION FIGHT AS EXPERT WARNS US COULD BE NEXT He said later: "This is what you get when you think that everyone is culturally and morally equivalent. They're not. And at some point, you have got to make the decision: Are we going to defend a Christian heritage in France, or are we not?" It comes after multiple days of violent protests and riots across France that have seen stores looted and centuries-old buildings burned and desecrated. France's secular centrist government has blamed far-left groups for exacerbating tension over high living costs and expensive education, among other issues. Self argued France was in an open "civil war" and said its military should step in, but was pessimistic that it would. WHO'S WHO: INSIDE FRANCE'S 'CHAOS INC.' FRANCHISE OF COMMUNIST GROUPS, LABOR UNIONS AND GLOBAL ACTIVISTS "There's too much destruction now, so we'll see if they've got the gumption to send in the military. But if they don't, then they're very close to losing their culture in the large cities," he said. Asked if the turmoil should force French President Emmanuel Macron to step down, Self said, "That's up to Macron. I think it would probably be beneficial to France." But he maintained the chaos should not turn into a backlash against the U.S.-France relationship — in fact, Self said, the U.S. ought to help France with intelligence-gathering about the protests. "I think we probably ought to offer them what help we could, facial identification, whatever," Self said, clarifying that he did not mean sending Americans in person. "France is still a very important, very large ally and partner. So we need to do what we can, understanding that, you know, President Trump has tried to get them to step up and do more. But this is not the time to abandon France." French authorities said 1,800 people were arrested nationwide, with over 800 of those arrested in the capital city of Paris alone. articles.title: The Affordable Care Act has proven unaffordable
articles.summary: A report from the Peterson-Kaiser Family Foundation indicates that ObamaCare premiums are projected to increase significantly through 2027, potentially triggering an insurance death spiral as enrollment declines following the expiration of enhanced subsidies.
articles.body:
Consumers are understandably grumbling that prices are way up on food and gasoline. But those price increases pale in comparison to the rise in Affordable Care Act (ObamaCare) premiums. And the situation will only get worse, raising the question of whether we should start calling it the Unaffordable Care Act?

A recent report from the Peterson-Kaiser Family Foundation surveyed 276 health insurers in all 50 states. It found the median ObamaCare premium increase for 2027 would be 15 percent. Nearly 90 of those insurers expected 2027 ObamaCare premiums to increase between 20 percent and 35 percent or more. And that’s after a 20 percent increase in 2026.

Thus, many people with ObamaCare coverage could see their premiums rise between 40 percent and 50 percent in just two years.

Democrats and most of the mainstream media want to blame President Trump and the Republicans for the increase. In fact, Democrats deserve virtually all the blame.

Democrats were warned — repeatedly. Those of us involved in health policy when ObamaCare passed predicted the price increases , which would lead to a declining number of covered individuals. Democrats disregarded the warnings and actuarial predictions, claiming they could make health insurance work the way they wanted it to work.

As ObamaCare’s Open Enrollment begins , the Kaiser Family Foundation is revealing just how many people have left or will likely leave ObamaCare.

According to Kaiser , “Enrollment in the individual health insurance market fell 18% between June 2025 and June 2026.” The “individual health insurance market” is where individuals who don’t have access to employer-based or government coverage buy their own health insurance, like they do auto and life insurance. Kaiser anticipates a decline of some 4.6 million people, out of about 20.5 million people.

One big factor causing the decline: “The enrollment decline coincides with the expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits and other policy changes that are expected to reduce enrollment,” according to Kaiser.

Just as consumers may buy less gas or food when prices go up, people enrolled in ObamaCare will increasingly drop coverage as the premiums rise. The dropouts will mostly be younger and healthier people who do not believe the increased cost of the premiums is worth the money, even if the premium is subsidized. That’s an economic and actuarial problem.

An insurance pool needs lots of healthy people who use little or no care paying premiums to offset the cost of a smaller number of people who use a lot of health care.

As younger and healthier individuals drop their coverage, that will leave the health insurance pool smaller and sicker, which will force premiums even higher, causing the next wave of dropouts. This cycle of rising premiums resulting in declining coverage is what in the insurance industry is known as the “ death spiral .”

This death spiral may be exacerbated by another problem. The Department of Health and Human Services announced in June, “Recent experience during and after the 2026 Open Enrollment Period strongly suggests ongoing and persistent fraud, waste, and abuse in the system. We estimate 2.6 million improper and phantom enrollments remain, including over 1 million enrollments without a Social Security number.”

As these “phantom enrollees” — that is, nonexistent or deceased people or people who have duplicate government coverage — are dropped from the ObamaCare rolls, their taxpayer-provided subsidies will cease. That will leave even less money to pay for the growing costs of a declining number of sicker ObamaCare enrollees. That development should accelerate the death spiral.

Democrats and the media have been blaming Republicans and President Trump for the rising premiums because Republicans did not renew ObamaCare’s enhanced subsidies. That’s misleading. ObamaCare premiums have been rising quickly because of the law’s structure and mandates.

ObamaCare included very generous subsidies when it passed in March 2010. Those subsidies are still in place. In 2021, as part of their pandemic spending, President Biden and his fellow Democrats passed legislation providing temporary, enhanced subsidies — subsidies on top of subsidies. It’s those temporary, enhanced subsidies that Republicans did not renew. The enhanced subsidies simply masked the real cost of the premium increases.

If the process continues as is, ObamaCare will soon become a very small program with mostly sick individuals, and the premiums will be significantly more expensive.

Can anything stop or reverse ObamaCare’s death spiral? Apart from a new round of enhanced subsidies, probably not.

If Democrats take control of Congress and the White House in the 2028 presidential election, they will almost surely try to pass another round of enhanced subsidies. With significantly enhanced subsidies, the insureds’ exodus would likely decline, not because ObamaCare is affordable, but because taxpayers are paying most of the cost.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.
