articles.title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS: ‘I haven’t gotten better’
articles.summary: Christina Applegate has revealed that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, putting her “back at square one.”
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Actress Christina Applegate has revealed that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, putting her “back at square one.”

In a two-part episode return to her podcast, “MeSsy,” Applegate, 54, shared that her doctor “came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.'” She had taken time away from “MeSsy,” which she co-hosts with Jamie Lynn Sigler of “The Sopranos,” to process the news.

“I was like, not happy at all,” Applegate recounted in the episodes, released Tuesday. “Everybody else was happy.”

An MS misdiagnosis is “fairly common,” Dr. Marwa Kaisey, associate professor with the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said in the episode. She explained that roughly 20% of those diagnosed with MS don’t have the disease, and that diagnosis is difficult because there is no single test for the condition.

Applegate explained that she is still experiencing difficult symptoms, and it’s not clear what is causing them.

“I haven’t gotten better, Jamie!” she said. “If anything, I’ve gotten worse. So I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me. And that’s going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into, just to find out what has been going on since 2021.”

Applegate revealed five years ago that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. She made rare public appearances afterward, including in 2023 when she attended what she called “my last awards show as an actor probably.”

MS causes the protective covering of nerves to break down, the Mayo Clinic explains . How it impacts a person can vary, but in more severe cases, patients can lose the ability to walk or move at all. In others, there can be months or years between attacks, which is known as remission. MS has no cure.

In the wake of her diagnosis, Applegate described herself and Sigler, who has relapsing multiple sclerosis, as “the poster children of MS.”

“I had a reason. I had a f—— reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason and it’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me,” she continued.

The actor added in the second part of the episodes released Tuesday that she had gone through “a great depression” because of her diagnosis.

“What do you say to someone who’s been living with this for six years … because it stopped my life,” Applegate said, explaining that she still has to use wheelchairs and struggles to walk. “Nothing magical happened when [the doctor] said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.”

articles.title: Bush family royalty backs Democrat in battle to flip Texas blue
articles.summary: Barbara Bush donated $2,500 to a PAC supporting James Talarico's Texas Senate race against Ken Paxton, using her real name in public FEC filings.
articles.body: Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico got a big-name boost from a surprising corner of the Republican Party as former first daughter Barbara Bush recently donated to the main PAC supporting his campaign. Former President George W. Bush has had a strained relationship with President Donald Trump dating back to the 2016 campaign, when Trump mocked both his mother and brother. But the donation by Bush’s daughter, the twin sister of NBC host Jenna Bush Hager, comes at a crucial time for Republicans’ hopes of holding the U.S. Senate. Fox News Digital confirmed through FEC filings that Barbara Bush — who shares the name of the late first lady, her grandmother — contributed $2,500 to Lone Star Rising PAC this quarter. The PAC accounts for almost all the outside spending supporting Talarico, according to Houston Public Media. TALARICO SAYS THE DIVIDE IS 'TOP VS. BOTTOM' — THEN HEADS TO ONE OF AMERICA'S RICHEST DONOR ENCLAVES While the amount is smaller than contributions from some other big-name donors, including The Eagles’ Don Henley, who gave $150,000 to the PAC, analysts said it is notable that Bush did not make an effort to conceal her politically famous identity. "She didn’t give it to a 501(c)(4), in which her contribution would’ve been completely anonymous. She gave it to a PAC that reports all the money in and out," Texas campaign finance expert Andrew Cates told Houston Public Media. GEORGE W BUSH RAISES MONEY FOR REPUBLICANS, BUT NOT KEY SENATE CANDIDATE Barbara Bush, 44, is currently an executive at the National Basketball Association, where she is vice president of social impact and inclusion. Her FEC filing reflected an address in Clinton Hill, Brooklyn. According to the George W. Bush Presidential Center, Bush works with the league internationally to use the "convening power of basketball" to support humanitarian efforts involving social justice, "health equity" and sustainability. She also co-founded the Global Health Corps geared toward empowering youth to solve global health issues. She and Hager also co-authored several children’s books. The George W. Bush Presidential Center did not respond to a request for comment directed to both former President Bush and Barbara Bush. Fox News Digital also reached out to the Washington Speakers Bureau, which represents Barbara Bush. Talarico has lambasted big money in politics and criticized Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and opponent Ken Paxton for "want[ing] corporations and billionaires to decide our elections, not Texans." articles.title: Abandoning Ukraine won’t fix Republicans’ midterm problems
articles.summary: Control of the House and Senate is rapidly slipping out of grasp for the Republican Party in the November midterm elections. With rising fuel costs at the top of voters’ minds, President Trump has committed to a questionable last resort: scapegoating Ukraine.
articles.body:
Control of the House and Senate is rapidly slipping out of grasp for the Republican Party in the November midterm elections. With rising fuel costs at the top of voters’ minds, President Trump has committed to a questionable last resort: scapegoating Ukraine.

Most economists agree that the war with Iran is the primary culprit for skyrocketing energy prices. Republican candidates in competitive races have broken with the president to call for the war to end, citing consumer stress at the gas pump.

However, that hasn’t stopped administration officials from attempting to shift blame from themselves to Ukraine.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent began promoting the narrative in early September, blaming Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for the global energy shock. Last week, Trump repeated the same talking point on Truth Social: “What’s driving up gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine.”

Trump then announced a deal with Russia that would include the immediate supply of 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets — a paltry figure that measures less than the daily consumption of the U.S. transport sector.

After immediate bipartisan backlash and public outcry, the agreement — framed as a relief package for the American people — was immediately tainted, appearing more like a unilateral concession to Russia and a petty swipe at Ukraine than an effort to support Americans hurt by rising prices.

The strategy was flawed on its face: Republicans, Democrats and independents hold overwhelmingly negative opinions of Russia. Bowing to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to lower energy prices just weeks before the midterms is a dangerous electoral exercise.

Even amid the backlash, Trump continued full throttle in his crusade against the Ukrainian government’s long-range strikes on Russian energy targets. Via Truth Social, Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to be removed from office, and announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.

The problem? Zelensky was completely unaware of the deal . Also, Russia violated the supposed ceasefire almost immediately after it was announced, hitting energy infrastructure across Ukraine.

Confusion is now mounting as to whether or not the U.S. will continue intelligence-sharing with Ukraine, after Zelensky claimed he received no prior American intelligence warning of Russian strikes last week that killed several people.

With nearly two-thirds of voters disapproving of Trump’s handling of foreign policy, this episode will only depress voter confidence in his pursuit to achieve a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, as well as his ability to manage global energy prices.

For Republican candidates in competitive races, the strategy is not winning over voters.

Polling in the past week has become so dire that Republicans have begun triaging House races in seats that were considered competitive just weeks ago. The Republican nominee for swing-state North Carolina, for example, Michael Whatley, currently has zero reserved TV ad slots .

Republican groups are being forced to spend millions to defend seats in states as conservative as South Carolina, where Republican Senate nominee Darline Graham has faced numerous attacks for her support of the war in Iran, despite its impact on fuel costs.

Republicans are in survival mode, yet Trump’s focus on punitive measures against Ukraine are unwavering. Voters hurting at the pump are not seeking finger-wagging at Zelensky — they are seeking relief. Instead, Trump is pursuing relief for Moscow. Over the weekend, the president suspended a slew of sanctions on Russia put forward by Graham in honor of her brother.

With inflation rising just weeks before the election and no sign of energy prices decreasing amid Trump’s unwavering campaign against Kyiv, relief for the American people is far away on the horizon.

And with inflation rising just weeks before the midterms, relief is far away on the horizon.

articles.title: FBI investigated whether Graham, Clyburn were involved in bribery scheme: Report
articles.summary: The FBI investigated whether South Carolina’s late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R) and Rep. James Clyburn (D) were involved in a bribery scheme in connection to Hawaiian naval defense contractor Navatek acquiring federal contracts in their home state, according to a report published by ProPublica on Tuesday. The report states that Graham met with two executives…
articles.body:
The FBI investigated whether South Carolina’s late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R) and Rep. James Clyburn (D) were involved in a bribery scheme in connection to Hawaiian naval defense contractor Navatek acquiring federal contracts in their home state, according to a report published by ProPublica on Tuesday.

The report states that Graham met with two executives and a lobbyist from Navatek in March 2020 and agreed to give a $10 million government contract to Navatek in South Carolina, Navatek CEO Martin Kao told the FBI. Graham allegedly asked that, in exchange, Kao pledge $100,000 to his reelection campaign.

The contractor also made similar alleged deals with Clyburn and Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.), a senior member of the House Armed Services Committee, after approaching their offices in early 2019, the outlet reported.

The FBI in early 2025 launched its investigation into alleged bribery in Congress, with Graham’s meeting with the Navatek executives and lobbyist at the heart of it. Agents interviewed Kao, who admitted his “business model consisted of bribing public officials in exchange for government contracts” and that Navatek’s research for the federal government “was often worthless,” ProPublica wrote.

Navatek was founded in 1979 and maintained close ties with former Sen. Daniel Inouye (D-Hawaii) but was “in need of a new patron in Washington” after his death in 2012, ProPublica wrote.

Kao planned to expand the defense contractor’s presence across the country to build new relationships with lawmakers via a plan he called “the method,” according to ProPublica. This led to opening offices in the states or districts of powerful lawmakers and partnering with local universities to develop proposals to receive federal research funding.

Navatek recruited the University of South Carolina for a joint research project and asked the lawmakers to provide $9.5 million for their work, with the aim of asking Congress to refresh the funding for two more years and approve two more projects for a total of $90 million, the outlet reported.

A final spending bill with the $9.5 million for Navatek’s project passed in December 2019. A Graham spokesperson told ProPublica that his office added the $9.5 million to the budget at the request of Navatek and the university, saying the research was supported by the Navy, but the spokesperson rejected the notion that Graham was motivated to fund Navatek’s research to acquire campaign funding.

Kao told the FBI that the scheme involved some of the most powerful members of Congress from both parties, with ProPublica noting that his admissions would “constitute a vast criminal bribery scheme if they could be proved in court.”

He spoke with the FBI in hopes of reducing his 2025 prison sentence, having pleaded guilty in 2022 to making illegal campaign donations and a loan fraud scheme.

Kao was sentenced to 87 months in prison.

FBI documents reviewed by the outlet showed that the admission lined up with records seized from Navatek, which named former Navatek executives Duke Hartman and Joshua Knight as subjects in the investigation. Hartman and Knight were never charged and later co-founded the naval research company called Integer Technologies.

“[It’s] corruption at its best,” Kao told ProPublica in his last statement to the outlet from federal detention in South Dakota. “But I am the only one rotting in prison.”

Graham, Clyburn and Wilson were not subjects in the investigation, though the FBI investigated their interactions with Kao, and agents said the lawmakers could be subjects in the future, according to records seen by ProPublica.

President Trump’s return to the White House led to the disbandment of many FBI and Justice Department teams that investigated public corruption, including the two agents investigating the bribery scheme. The case is effectively dead with none of its investigators left at the agency.

The Hill has reached out to the FBI for comment.

Graham’s former communications director, Taylor Reidy, who holds the same role under his sister Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), told ProPublica that the allegations of “quid-pro-quo behavior or wrongdoing … are simply false” and called Kao’s remarks the “ravings of a convicted felon.” She said the FBI never contacted the late senator’s office.

“Whatever a donor may think or say, a donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Jami LaRue, Clyburn’s communications director, told the outlet.

“The Congressman has always striven to assist the University of South Carolina and all of the colleges and universities in his district when called upon to further their important missions,” LaRue added. “The crimes and lies of an imprisoned fraudster will not cause the Congressman to waver in his support for these fine institutions.”

Wilson’s communications director David Snider said the House member “has always abided by campaign donation regulations set forth by the Federal Election Commission.”

articles.title: Mississippi attorney general says officer was justified in shooting that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley
articles.summary: The Mississippi attorney general’s office said in a statement Monday that a state investigation found the use of force was “justified” in an officer-involved shooting in June that took the life of a 1-year-old boy. While responding to a shoplifting call at a Walmart in Senatobia, an officer fired at a moving vehicle, killing Kohen…
articles.body:
The Mississippi attorney general’s office said in a statement Monday that a state investigation found the use of force was “justified” in an officer-involved shooting in June that took the life of a 1-year-old boy.

While responding to a shoplifting call at a Walmart in Senatobia, an officer fired at a moving vehicle, killing Kohen Wiley, The Associated Press reported .

Officers believed the boy’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, and a friend stole diapers and baby clothes. Wiley was carrying her son as she and the friend exited the store, got into a car and began driving away. An officer then fired into the moving vehicle.

Wiley has denied the allegations, and court records show neither she nor her friend was charged with shoplifting or any other counts, according to the AP .

Following the shooting, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation released a statement saying officers tried to stop the vehicle, but it drove toward them, prompting one of the officers to fire into the car, striking the toddler and his mother’s friend.

Martin Zummach, an attorney representing the officer, told the AP the attorney general’s findings cleared his client of criminal wrongdoing. Zummach said the driver of the vehicle “tried to kill” his client and other officers who were present, leaving the officer no choice but to fire his weapon.

Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney representing Kohen’s family, called for authorities to release video footage of the encounter to support the attorney general’s finding that the shooting was a justified use of force, according to the AP report.

The shooting incident ignited outrage and tension between the police and Black residents in the small town of Senatobia, leading to protests and calls for greater police accountability.

Marquell Bridges, an activist who has been working with Kohen’s family, also called for the release of video footage of the shooting in a statement, according to the AP.

“His family deserves the truth. The public deserves transparency,” Bridges said in the AP report. “We will not be silent. We will not look away. And we will not allow the life of a Black child to be treated as though it means nothing.”

articles.title: Trump and Vance to announce a $25M whistleblower program to encourage public to report alleged fraud
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are set Tuesday to announce a $25 million program to encourage the public to blow the wh...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance are set Tuesday to announce a $25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government as they ramp up an existing effort to end the abuse of federal programs and dollars.

Under the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP, anyone who submits a tip to fraud.gov that leads to a fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action is eligible to receive up to $30,000, the White House said. The Justice Department will administer the program.

The Republican president has undertaken an aggressive effort to eliminate fraud throughout the government. Trump established a task force on the topic in March and put Vance in charge of it.

They are scheduled to announce the fund during a joint appearance in the Oval Office later Tuesday.

"Every day, President Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars and giving Americans the accountability they deserve. This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans," said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.

During the Oval Office event, Trump will present a $10,000 check to Nick Shirley, a right-wing influencer who posted a video last year that said members of Minnesota's Somali community were running fake childcare centers to collect federal subsidies.

The video caught the attention of the Trump administration and conservative activists, though inspectors said the centers were operating as expected . Investigations, searches and arrests followed.

In July, one woman, Fahima Mahamud, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States by submitting inflated reimbursement claims for meals allegedly served to children at her childcare center, according to the Justice Department.

The White House says Mahamud was featured in Shirley's video.

articles.title: Trump uses antisemitic slur at Kansas rally
articles.summary: President Trump used an antisemitic slur at a rally in Kansas on Monday while defending Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) over revelations he sued his patients for unpaid medical bills. Trump has defended Marshall for going after the unpaid bills, saying he was “mandated by law” to do so. “He was mandated by law to request,…
articles.body:
President Trump used an antisemitic slur at a rally in Kansas on Monday while defending Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) over revelations he sued his patients for unpaid medical bills.

Trump has defended Marshall for going after the unpaid bills, saying he was “mandated by law” to do so.

“He was mandated by law to request, strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it, you have to by law go after those people,” the president said, going on to use an antisemitic slur to describe how he felt the reporting characterized Marshall.

Marshall is in a competitive Senate race in Kansas against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, gives Marshall a 65 percent chance of winning reelection.

The president used the slur before during remarks at a bill signing for his signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in July 2025. He said the slur while speaking about allowing farmers to pay reduced estate taxes.

When asked about his use of the slur, Trump at the time said he had “never heard it that way” and said he viewed the use of the word differently.

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Trump and Republicans have attempted to court Jewish voters this cycle, hitting Democrats in some key races for their views on Israel. CNN’s chief data analyst Harry Enten recently pointed to surveys of Jewish voters in New York, which has a significant Jewish population, showing Democrats losing support.

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL), a nonprofit advocating against antisemitism, said in July 2025 that the slur “evokes a centuries-old antisemitic trope about Jews and greed.”

The term Trump used originates from William Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice,” which features a Jewish character of the same name who extended a loan to a merchant and said he would cut off the merchant’s flesh if it was not repaid.

The ADL wrote last year that the slur “evokes a centuries-old antisemitic trope about Jews and greed that is extremely offensive and dangerous,” adding, “President Trump’s use of the term is very troubling and irresponsible.”

In a new statement Tuesday morning, the ADL reiterated that the slur was offensive but did not name the president directly.

“Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community,” the ADL wrote.

Former President Biden also used the slur in 2014 while vice president and later apologized for doing so.

From voter education to grassroots organizing, we remain committed to building informed, engaged…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris and the NAACP are set to host midterm town halls to drive voters in swing states to the polls amid speculation about a 2028 presidential bid from Harris.

“Our work doesn’t begin or end on Election Day. From voter education to grassroots organizing, we remain committed to building informed, engaged communities,” said Derrick Johnson, President and CEO of the NAACP. “We look forward to continuing that work alongside Vice President Harris in Milwaukee and Atlanta.”

Harris is slated to take the stage on Oct. 26 in Milwaukee, Wis. as the state decides who will take the state’s open gubernatorial seat after Gov. Tony Evers (D) announced his retirement.

On Oct. 29, the former vice president will appear in Atlanta, Ga. as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) fights to retain his seat for a second term against Rep. Mike Collins (R).

While Harris recently said she was “ undecided ” on a presidential run, many see her as a top contender to serve as Democrats’ nominee, recent polls suggest. Harris said in February that she “might” run in 2028.

A Focaldata/Financial Times poll found 30 percent of respondents chose Harris as the next presidential Democratic nominee over other popular choices such California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Newsom has been honest about not running for president if Harris decides to, and Ocasio-Cortez told the New York Times that she thinks about the possibility of running for president “ personally .”

Harris has embarked on a campaign blitz in October before Election Day with other stops in Mississippi and New Hampshire, according to her office.

“‘28 don’t matter if we don’t do ‘26 right. What’s right in front of us,” Harris added when talking with actress Keke Palmer.

articles.title: The high cost of Trump’s backward fuel policy
articles.summary: American consumers will pay dearly for this misguided decision.
articles.body:
Five decades ago, when the United States faced unusually high fuel prices and energy-security concerns from the slowdown of Middle East exports, President Ford successfully urged Congress to pass the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. This bipartisan legislation gave the national highway authority the ability to promulgate fuel efficiency standards, which have reduced Americans’ fuel costs while also producing significant environmental and climate change benefits ever since.

Now, the United States faces similar concerns with fuel prices and energy security, self-inflicted as a result of President Trump’s decision to attack Iran . But this time, the administration has eviscerated Congress’s solution.

Last month, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration significantly weakened the existing Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards, even ones that had already been met. Possibly attempting to offset some of the resulting cost increases, Trump has now announced that the United States will buy diesel from Russia, breaking a blockade and assisting one of our principal foreign adversaries.

But the fuel-economy rollback will have a far larger effect on consumers.

The administration’s justifications for weakening fuel economy do not withstand even cursory scrutiny. Its principal explanation is that lowering the CAFE standards will lower the average sticker price of new cars, by about $1,300. It turns out, however, that car owners would pay more than this amount in additional fuel costs over the course of five years.

Trump brushes aside this inconvenient fact by arguing that higher prices would stand in the way of Americans’ ability to purchase new cars. This assertion is also highly misleading: the higher fuel costs resulting from this policy would exceed the lower monthly payments on the loans over that same five-year period. Every month, the approximately 85 percent of Americans who finance the purchase of a new car would be worse off as a direct result of the Trump administration’s decision-making.

The administration also states that that because lenders “base financing decisions on loan-to-value ratios and will not extend more credit to account for future fuel savings” related to CAFE standards, the rollback will enable Americans to buy new cars that they otherwise would not be able to afford. But this argument is specious.

The average price of a new car is around $50,000. So, the scenario that the Trump administration highlights applies only to purchasers who would not qualify for a $50,000 loan but would qualify for a $48,700 loan — likely a very small group. And those purchasers, like all other borrowers, would be worse off as a result of the CAFE standards rollback, because their combined loan and fuel payments each month will be higher than they otherwise would have been.

Purchasers of new cars are not the only car owners hurt by this rollback, however. The increased demand for fuel increases prices for all consumers, including ones who are not contemplating buying new cars. Like many other policies out of the Trump administration, this one hurts many working-class Americans, for whom buying a new car is not a short-term option and who will now be continuously burdened by higher prices at the pump.

Perhaps sensing that it should try to take action to counteract the negative effects resulting from its CAFE standards rollback, the administration announced last week that the United States would purchase diesel from Russia, thereby attempting to reduce the price of this fuel. The move was sharply criticized by a bipartisan group of prominent senators, who decried it as a violation of a congressionally imposed ban on energy imports from Russia and a “financial lifeline” for Vladimir Putin’s war aims. Despite the serious geopolitical consequences of the action, the amount of diesel purchased from Russia is far less than the additional fuel consumption that will result from the rollback of the CAFE standards.

In erasing fuel economy standards, the Trump administration is doing precisely the opposite of what Congress intended when it enacted the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to address a past fuel crisis. This move will saddle Americans with higher costs that cannot be fixed with a highly troubling deal for Russian diesel.

Richard L. Revesz, the AnBryce Professor of Law and dean emeritus at New York University School of Law, served as the administrator of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs from Jan. 3, 2023, to Jan. 20, 2025.

articles.title: Vance says he thinks Trump will endorse him if he runs
articles.summary: Vice President Vance said on Monday that if he runs for the GOP presidential nomination in 2028, President Trump “would endorse” him amid speculation over whether he will announce a bid. “I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” Vance…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance said on Monday that if he runs for the GOP presidential nomination in 2028, President Trump “would endorse” him amid speculation over whether he will announce a bid.

“I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” Vance said in an interview with 2WAY . “And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let like this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”

“Like sometimes you know media scrutiny, pressure, policy. I can be terrible at it, and that is the sort of thing that maybe you know, so I don’t know,” he continued.

Vance stated he had never spoken with Trump about potentially running for president, adding, “if I run, I think the president would endorse me. But I also haven’t talked to him about it yet.”

The vice president has reiterated multiple times he is focused on the 2026 midterm election, though many see him as the heir apparent to the Republican Party after Trump exits the White House.

A Focaldata/Financial Times poll found 38 percent of respondents picked Vance as the Republican nominee in 2028 over his perceived top contender , Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Trump has also repeatedly egged on the competition between Vance and Rubio for the 2028 Republican nomination. Vance even jokingly likened the competition to the president’s former reality show, “The Apprentice.”

Rubio told donors and other allies that he will not run, particularly against Vance, sources told The Hill .

The vice president has also appeared at numerous rallies alongside Trump on his red state campaign blitz, with one Republican operative telling The Hill that he “will continue to be another fantastic surrogate on the trail.”

“He’s able to reach voters where they’re at across the Midwest and beyond,” the Republican operative added.

In August, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) denied that the Republican Party had coalesced around Vance as a 2028 nominee, saying the party will first have a “full discussion about who we are and what we believe.”

articles.title: Macron jets out of riot-torn France for Gulf trip as political pressure mounts
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron left for Kuwait energy talks as riots raged, drawing sharp criticism from Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron pressed ahead with a trip to the Arabian Gulf as violent riots rocked France, fueling fresh criticism of his leadership as his government struggled to contain the unrest. What began weeks earlier as purportedly student-led demonstrations over classroom conditions escalated into widespread riots involving a range of political and ideological factions across France over the weekend. Images and videos posted to social media on Saturday and Sunday showed groups of men waving foreign flags while engaging in acts of destruction on the streets of France's major cities. A Fox News Digital investigation found that communist organizations, Islamic advocacy groups, labor unions and environmental activists were involved in the unrest. Amid this backdrop, Macron was planning a trip to the Arabian Gulf for energy negotiations. The chaos in his country did not dissuade him from traveling. He left for Kuwait on Sunday, shortly after denouncing the "unbridled" violence of the rioters in a nationwide address. WHERE'S MACRON? FRENCH LEADER BLASTED FOR ATTENDING CONCERT AS RIOTS ESCALATED The French president, defending his travel to the Arabian Gulf, noted that heightened fuel prices were, in his telling, one of the causes behind the ongoing riots. French officials say that they have arrested over 2,500 people in connection with the demonstrations. Though Macron acknowledges failures in security, he declined the resignation of his interior minister. Macron received criticism from the left and the right for his handling of the riots. Marine Le Pen, a right-wing contender for the presidency, charged that France under Macron was a country "caught in a vice between violence and impotence." From the left, socialist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Macron’s government of relying on "inaction and police brutality" to quell the riots. FRANCE'S MASSIVE INTEL FAILURE SPARKS RESIGNATION OFFERS AMID DAYS OF RIOTING The demonstrations occurred as France’s presidential election looms. Macron is term-limited, and his centrist allies face an increasingly difficult political environment as figures including Le Pen on the right and Mélenchon on the left seek to capitalize on growing discontent. Political observers have suggested that the riots could help Le Pen, a staunch critic of immigration, at the polls. Macron was also criticized for attending a concert as the riots were ongoing. VIOLENT FAR-LEFT RIOTS IN FRANCE ARE 'CHILLING WARNING' FOR AMERICANS AT HOME, MIKE JOHNSON SAYS Violence in the streets of France has reportedly cooled after officials implemented overnight curfews in Paris and other major cities. That was not before rioters inflicted over $1 billion in estimated damages, including by destroying small businesses and setting fire to historic buildings, according to an analysis from the financial services firm Morningstar. The unrest in France struck a particular chord with American conservatives, who saw it as emblematic of a broader decline in European social cohesion and as a cautionary tale for Americans. Simon Hankinson, former U.S. consul in Marseille, called the riots a "warning sign for the United States." Conservative commentator Ben Shapiro blamed the demonstrations on "an out-of-control welfare state, left-wing radicalism and third world immigration. "Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," Vice President JD Vance wrote on X. "They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn't listen." Ro Khanna, have pointed to economic grievances as a driving force behind the unrest, although Khanna condemned the violence and vandalism that accompanied the demonstrations.

articles.title: France could face even worse destruction with second weekend of planned riots, State Dept warns

articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The State Department warns that antifascist groups are planning to participate in a "potentially more confrontational protest" this weekend as the far-right National Rally holds its political convention just days after widespread riots overwhelmed police and exposed major security failures. As party leader Marine Le Pen prepares for the gathering on Oct. 24–25 in Orléans, France, an internal document obtained by Fox News Digital cautions that antagonists are planning more demonstrations near the convention venue that could "expose further security shortcomings and deepen political tensions." The warning comes at a particularly dangerous political moment for President Emmanuel Macron, considering the same unrest that exposed his government's security vulnerabilities could also give National Rally and center-right parties an opening to challenge his record, according to the State Department assessment. GLOBAL 'CHAOS INC' GROWS TO 101 GROUPS WITH PLANS FOR NEW ROUNDS OF DEMONSTRATIONS Now, French authorities face another high-stakes security test as demonstrators prepare to converge on the congress of a party that could benefit politically from the previous unrest. The demonstrations are expected to coincide with the National Rally's two-day party congress, where Le Pen is set to launch her presidential campaign. Left-wing parties, unions and activist groups are planning a march Saturday, while antifascist groups have announced plans for a separate protest Sunday near the convention venue, according to the State Department assessment. WHO'S WHO: INSIDE FRANCE'S 'CHAOS INC.' FRANCHISE OF COMMUNIST GROUPS, LABOR UNIONS AND GLOBAL ACTIVISTS National Rally President Jordan Bardella has ruled out canceling the congress, while local authorities are preparing additional security restrictions around the gathering. The looming confrontation comes as France is still reeling from the Oct. 17 unrest, when authorities badly underestimated the scale of demonstrations that descended into widespread rioting and looting. Some 550,000 people joined 110 marches nationwide, according to France's Interior Ministry. More than 2,400 people were arrested, nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured and thousands of businesses were damaged. And intelligence failures that far underestimated the turnout left authorities overwhelmed and facing more than double the number of protesters originally estimated. The State Department's internal assessment notes that the violence has reshaped France's political debate just six months before voters choose Macron's successor. It says the unrest has shifted attention away from the economic and education grievances that initially drove the protests and toward public security and government accountability, potentially giving National Rally and center-right parties an opening to challenge Macron's record. French officials have acknowledged that intelligence and planning failures contributed to authorities being overwhelmed during the Oct. 17 unrest. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation after acknowledging police "lost control" in some major cities. Macron rejected it, citing the need for continuity in law enforcement command, and ordered "full transparency" over the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that preceded the violence. Nuñez has said authorities need to improve their ability to anticipate large-scale mobilizations, putting added pressure on security services to avoid a repeat when demonstrators converge on Orléans this weekend. And the government may have little time to recover even if the National Rally congress passes without major violence. Labor organizations are already mobilizing for nationwide strikes and demonstrations Nov. 5 over wages, public services and the proposed 2027 budget, according to the State Department document. The internal assessment said Macron faces competing pressure to restore order while addressing the grievances fueling the protests, with limited fiscal room for concessions as parliament debates next year's budget. articles.title: Hinojosa sues for emails between Abbott, Musk
articles.summary: Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) filed a lawsuit on Monday to force her opponent in the state’s gubernatorial race, Gov. Greg Abbott (R), to release his emails with Republican ally Elon Musk. The complaint accuses Abbott of violating state public records law by refusing to provide Hinojosa with requested documents of the governor’s exchanges…
articles.body:
Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D) filed a lawsuit on Monday to force her opponent in the state’s gubernatorial race, Gov. Greg Abbott (R), to release his emails with Republican ally Elon Musk.

The complaint accuses Abbott of violating state public records law by refusing to provide Hinojosa with requested documents of the governor’s exchanges with the Tesla and SpaceX founder.

Last year, the governor’s office shared nearly 1,400 pages in response to a public records request from The Texas Newsroom for Abbott’s communications with Musk. The vast majority of these documents were completely redacted.

Lawyers for Abbott and Musk fought against the release of these documents, arguing they would reveal trade secrets, confidential legal and policymaking discussions and potentially “intimate and embarrassing” messages.

In the lawsuit, Hinojosa notes that she requested to review the unredacted version of these messages “for legislative purposes,” noting that state law bars her from publicly releasing the redacted content.

The Democratic gubernatorial candidate said she has a “right to see” these documents during a Monday press conference announcing the new complaint.

“This is in-our-face corruption,” she said. “It is a governor and a government doing the bidding of the moneyed interest, the biggest money in the world, instead of the people of Texas and leaving the people of Texas to fend for themselves. That is what this election is about. That is what this lawsuit is about.”

In a statement to The Hill, an Abbott spokesperson called the lawsuit “baseless” and “nothing more than an act of desperation.”

Hinojosa and Abbott are locked in a competitive race for the state’s top executive office. In a Marist survey conducted earlier this month, the incumbent Republican posted a 4-point advantage over his Democratic challenger that was within the poll’s margin of error.

articles.title: 18-year-old accused of planning Mall of America terror attack will remain in jail

U.S. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster said Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud,18, won’t be released because he’s a risk to the community and a flight risk, the Associated…
articles.body:
A Minnesota teen who was arrested after being accused of planning a terror attack on the Mall of America in Minneapolis must remain in jail, a federal judge ruled Monday.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Dulce Foster said Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud,18, won’t be released because he’s a risk to the community and a flight risk, the Associated Press reported .

During an almost two-year undercover investigation by the FBI , Mohamud traded messages with a confidential informant and paid $600 to an FBI employee posing as a member of ISIS for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition. He was arrested on Oct. 6 in a public park following the purchase.

According to a federal complaint described by U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen, Mohamud texted a confidential FBI source and repeatedly conveyed his intent to carry out an attack to kill non-Muslims.

“This was as close to committing a terrorist attack as he could have gotten,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Bejar said during the hearing according to the AP. “He was 100% committed to doing this crime and he was 100% committed to doing it on behalf of ISIS.”

Mohamud’s attorney Manny Atwal said during Monday’s hearing that he was just 16 when the confidential informant began speaking to him. She further argued that his only access to weapons was through those supplied by the FBI.

Atwal had asked for Mohamud to be held in a halfway house where he would be monitored by GPS and have no access to the internet.

FBI Special Agent Keegan Rupenthal, who testified at Monday’s hearing, said Mohamud’s ultimate goal was to become a martyr and during his arrest he pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group’s leader, the AP noted.

articles.title: Republicans raised $1.2 billion to reach young voters. Democrats must respond.
articles.summary: The difference between a blue ripple and a blue wave will be the turnout of young voters.
articles.body:
Democrats are poised to have a good election night in November, but the difference between a blue ripple and a blue wave will be the turnout of young voters. Given the electoral landscape right now, young voter turnout could easily determine control of the Senate and whether Democrats’ House majority is a true governing one.

On the left, there is frightening underinvestment in youth organizing, paid media and online engagement programs. It began with the right’s massive $1.2 billion investment in youth in 2024, outspending the left 10 to 1. This trend has continued, with many efforts from the left’s ecosystem short on money for youth programs at the exact time when Trump’s approval with young voters is cratering.

Of the lessons the swing to the right of youth — especially non-college young men — in 2024 taught us, not one of them was that less investment would yield better results.

Young people across the board are with Democrats — we have seen in how they voted in 2025 and consistently across polling in the last few months. Students and young women have always been a base constituency for Democrats. Young men who supported Trump in 2024 are “ swinging away hard from Republicans ” and Trump largely based on the Iran War and the economy.

In battleground Senate races like Texas and Michigan , young people prefer the Democratic candidates anywhere from 20 to 31 points. That advantage is even larger among students: Democrats have a 52-point lead on the generic ballot, according to flytedesk’s September student survey .

But at the same time, we cannot assume young people will turn out to vote. Young people are about 21 points to 27 points less motivated to vote in this off-year election compared to older, more right-leaning voters, even in battleground states. In the last midterm, Gen Z was especially likely to skip the election without intervention, with only 28 percent voting in 2022 compared to 50 percent in 2024.

Turnout among young voters is also very elastic. According to the Voter Participation Center , between 2020 and 2024, turnout among voters under age 35 declined almost 7 percent, representing 2.5 million young voters. Moreover, 40 percent of Gen Z and 36 percent of people under age 35 are not registered to vote — 11 percent among both groups were registered to vote but did not turn out to vote in 2024.

This registration gap and turnout elasticity problem is magnified by the fact that young people are also extremely mobile and face unique challenges to voting as first-time voters.

As of 2025 , 36 percent of voters under age 35 reported having moved in the last two years, and 52 percent reported having moved in the last four years. Just looking at college students in the top battleground states, we have almost 1 million who cross state lines to attend college , not to mention those who move within the state they grew up in for school.

Republican election officials have made it harder for students to vote by denying on-campus polling sites and restricting student IDs across the country, including in North Carolina and New Hampshire . But young organizers are fighting back, whether that be the North Carolina College Democrats making sure students know about polling site changes or the Voters of Tomorrow’s Virginia chapter getting a polling site approved on campus at Hampton University.

Young voters are both one of the most valuable and hardest-to-reach audiences with conventional programs: They don’t watch local news or answer the phone. They live inside a dense web of private group chats, dorm threads, student org servers and campus-specific communities that no traditional broadcast buy, canvasser or ad account can enter.

The most effective way to reach them is through individuals and channels who are already there and already trusted. Luckily, groups nationwide have built the groundwork needed to maximize turnout among young voters.

Republicans have poured over a billion dollars to reach young people. Democrats need to take this threat seriously. Young voters will vote for Democrats by and large, but that’s only if they actually turn out. Twenty-eight states either allow same-day voter registration or have deadlines within 15 days of Election Day. The battle for the youth vote is far from over.

Celinda Lake is a veteran Democratic pollster. Eve Levenson is the chair of the board for Voters of Tomorrow and was National Youth Vote director for the 2024 Harris-Walz campaign.

articles.title: Winery owned by Ilhan Omar's husband shuttered due to fraud, James Comer says
articles.summary: Tim Mynett's winery eStCru allegedly sold empty barrels to investors, James Comer says, as Rep. Ilhan Omar faces a federal citizenship probe.
articles.body: A winery co-owned by the husband of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was shuttered amid fraud claims, House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., said. Comer said over the weekend that the winery had been selling empty barrels to investors under the guise of "wine to be aged." "I can tell you from our initial investigation of Omar and her financial disclosure form that there are multiple fronts where you could get a search warrant issued," Comer told Trey Gowdy on Fox News' "Sunday Night in America." "First of all, not only was there a huge discrepancy in the financial disclosure form, there was the winery that was the big base of her $25 million listing on her financial disclosure form. That winery has, according to the press, been shut down because of fraud." ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION The winery, co-owned by the congresswoman's husband, Tim Mynett, shut down in April this year amid congressional scrutiny over Omar's finances. OMAR'S DISCLOSURES ERASED MILLIONS, LEAVING HER WITH POTENTIAL NEGATIVE NET WORTH. SHE WON'T EXPLAIN WHY The revelation is not new, but it's one of several details that have resurfaced in recent days amid a federal probe into Omar's citizenship in the U.S. Federal law enforcement executed a search warrant at her D.C. home earlier this month. The operation was linked to allegations that she and her father misrepresented the congresswoman's age to more easily obtain American citizenship. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Omar's critics, like House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., have called for the progressive Democrat to be deported if the allegations were proved true. She and her allies have denied wrongdoing and attacked the investigation as a partisan hit job against one of President Donald Trump's most vocal opponents. But it's not the first time Omar has faced accusations of impropriety as a member of Congress. The House Oversight Committee had earlier probed Omar's finances after her public disclosures showed a rapid, and at the time unexplained, increase in her net worth. Omar previously chalked up the discrepancy to an accidental accounting error. Comer zeroed in on the winery in a February letter sent just weeks before the business closed down. He wrote to Mynett that Omar's 2023 financial disclosure forms "lists a stake in your winery eStCru worth between $15,001 and $50,000." The following year, her financial disclosure form listed a stake in eStCru "worth between $1,000,001 and $5,000,000." TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID "There are serious public concerns about how your businesses increased so dramatically in value only a year after reporting very limited assets," the letter said. Omar told The Wall Street Journal in mid-April that she and her husband have less than $100,000 combined. The winery, eStCru, was based in California and was founded in 2020 by Mynett and a business partner. The industry outlet Wine Business named it one of its "Hot Brands of 2022." When asked about the probe, a spokesperson for the House Oversight Committee pointed out to Fox News Digital that Comer had referred the case of Omar's finances to the House Ethics Committee for review. "Regarding the investigation into her spouse, the House Oversight Committee referred the matter months ago to the House Ethics Committee and encouraged it to do its job and review the concerning allegations," the spokesperson said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The bipartisan panel is tasked with investigating accusations of impropriety by lawmakers and recommending punishments if those probes turn up wrongdoing. It has not yet taken up Omar's case.

articles.title: Former Minnesota GOP governor sees ‘political layer’ to Omar probe
articles.summary: Tim Pawlenty, the former Republican governor of Minnesota, acknowledged on Tuesday morning there was a “political layer” to the Trump administration’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.). Federal agents searched the Democrat’s Washington, D.C., home on Oct. 12 as part of an ongoing criminal probe into allegations of fraud and false statements made in immigration…
articles.body:
Tim Pawlenty, the former Republican governor of Minnesota, acknowledged on Tuesday morning there was a “political layer” to the Trump administration’s investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).

Federal agents searched the Democrat’s Washington, D.C., home on Oct. 12 as part of an ongoing criminal probe into allegations of fraud and false statements made in immigration paperwork. The raid sparked broad condemnation from Democrats, who pointed to the close proximity of the midterm elections.

“The timing of it does suggest a political layer to it,” Pawlenty told CNN’s Kate Bolduan on “CNN This Morning. “Of course, because it’s political doesn’t mean it isn’t necessarily meritorious.”

He noted that the judge who signed the search warrant, D.C. District Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, previously clerked for Democratic officials.

“I don’t know whether there’s something real here or not,” Pawlenty said. “All of us are just going to have to wait until the actual evidence is produced.”

Omar, a longtime target of President Trump and his administration, decried the raid as an attempt of “political intimidation” in a social media post.

Additionally, Bolduan pressed Pawlenty about the president repeatedly calling Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) “ Mohammed .”

The Michigan-born Democratic nominee’s middle name is Mohamed — a fact Trump admitted during a speech at a Monday political rally in Kansas he did not know before.

“Actually his middle name is Mohamed, if you can believe it. It’s true,” the president said. “The one good thing, if you call somebody from that part of the world Mohamed, you’re about 65 percent sure to get it right.”

El-Sayed and other Democrats have accused Trump of using his Muslim faith against him.

“He knows my middle name is Abdul. He says it everyday,” the Democratic nominee wrote on social media after the president called him “Mohammed El-Sayed” in a Truth Social post earlier this month.

“But he’s not just attacking me. He’s attacking all of us,” El-Sayed added. “He thinks so low of us.”

Pawlenty expressed his desire to see the president home in on addressing concerns about his administration’s ongoing military operations against Iran and rising energy prices amid this conflict.

“I wish he would focus more on the main issue at the moment, which is what are we going to do about these rising costs in our economy?” the former governor said.

articles.title: 7 in 10 doubt Trump would accept GOP losses in midterms: Survey
articles.summary: A new poll shows that most Americans surveyed doubt President Trump will accept the midterm election results if Republicans sustain losses in Congress and lose their majority. The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll found that 70 percent of respondents are not confident Trump will accept the results, including 36 percent of Republicans, 77 percent of independents…
articles.body:
A new poll shows that most Americans surveyed doubt President Trump will accept the midterm election results if Republicans sustain losses in Congress and lose their majority.

The Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll found that 70 percent of respondents are not confident Trump will accept the results, including 36 percent of Republicans, 77 percent of independents and 94 percent of Democrats.

There’s confidence among 28 percent of respondents that Trump will accept the midterm results. Sixty-three percent of Republicans are confident Trump will accept the results, as are 21 percent of independents, while 6 percent of Democrats are confident he will accept the results.

Democratic leaders are largely considered likely to approve of the results, according to 61 percent of respondents to the poll. The majority of Democrats, at 88 percent, are confident their party leaders will accept the results if they sustain losses, as are 58 percent of independents. Pollsters found that 36 percent of Republicans think Democratic leaders will accept election losses.

A majority of Democrats polled, at 70 percent, and 67 percent of Republicans say they are confident, however, that the elections will be fair and accurate.

The poll also shows that 60 percent of all respondents are somewhat or very confident that the midterms will be conducted fairly; 51 percent of independents say they are confident compared to the 47 percent who say they are not.

Pollsters found that GOP confidence leading into the midterms is higher than their outlook on the 2024 election, when 49 percent said the votes would be counted accurately. After the election, 77 percent of Republicans said there was no evidence of voter fraud and nearly all said Trump’s victory was legitimate, according to a Washington Post-University of Maryland poll at the time.

Trump has frequently criticized the legitimacy of U.S. elections. He doubted his loss in the Iowa Republican presidential caucus to Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in 2016, accusing the senator of cheating and calling for a recount . These doubts continued, leading up to his unfounded claims of voter fraud following his loss to former President Biden in 2020.

The Justice Department (DOJ) has sought to investigate the president’s claims, recently charging 28 California voters who are allegedly not U.S. citizens. The crimes include fraudulently registering to vote in U.S. elections, with the majority of the 28 voting with “illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots,” the DOJ said on Monday.

The DOJ sued California on Thursday after providing state and local election officials with a USB drive containing voter roll citizenship data, giving the state 48 hours to compare 20,000 names the Department of Homeland Security flagged as non-U.S. citizens with its own data rolls. DOJ officials warned California officials of criminal charges if they did not include the names of those alleged non-citizens.

“They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post last Friday, sharing a copy of a letter the DOJ sent to the Los Angeles County Counsel’s Office.

The Post-ABC News-Ipsos survey was conducted Oct. 9-13 and included 2,545 respondents. The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

articles.title: ‘You have to sacrifice’: Trump voters stay loyal as US midterms approach
articles.summary: Rising economic pain confronting US voters has not translated into a loss of faith among Trump’s most loyal supporters.
articles.body:
McConnellsburg, Pennsylvania, USA – Calvin Ott, the owner of a landscaping business in a consistent stronghold for United States President Donald Trump, is one of several so-called “MAGA voters” whose support has not wavered – even as life has gotten a lot more expensive since the president returned to office last year.

“I’m 75 years old, and I’m still working,” Ott says as he sips his Coors Light beer under the dim lights of Fulton Pub in McConnellsburg.

The pub, which serves as a watering hole for the town’s approximately 1,000 residents, is where Ott unwinds after his doctor’s appointment before making the one-hour drive back through the Appalachian Mountains to his home in Shippensburg.

“I had quadruple bypasses. I’ve had skin cancer. I have my fingers cut off. I’ve had several heart issues”, Ott said with a bit of pride, showing off his right hand that has fallen victim to decades of chainsaw and lawnmower accidents.

Despite rising medical costs – his medications have more than doubled in price since last year – and his inability to retire as he approaches his 80s, the three-time Trump voter said he will continue to vote for Republicans in next month’s US midterm elections.

“I support him 100 percent,” Ott told Al Jazeera as Foreigner’s song Urgent played in the background of the pub.

In 2016, less than 6,000 people in Fulton County, where the town is located, supported Trump’s presidential campaign. That number rose to more than 7,000 eight years later, helping to fuel Trump’s return to the White House.

For Ott, his support is less a reflection of what Trump has done than what Democrats would do if they were in power.

“He’s the only president that made a promise that he kept,” Ott said. “He hates wars, even though we’re in one. But he’s for America.”

“What the hell did Biden ever give out?” he railed about the economic policies of Trump’s Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, which included a $1,400 stimulus cheque to Americans through legislation during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The unrelenting support for Trump among his most loyal supporters runs through Republican strongholds like McConnellsburg.

MAGA voters like Ott make up the backbone of the president’s support: working-class, white, without college degrees, and angry with Washington.

A poll conducted last month by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17 percent of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while slightly more than a quarter of those surveyed approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Trump’s most fervent supporters say their frustrations – and economic burden – have only grown since Trump’s re-election. But unlike most Americans, they don’t blame the president for the country’s economic woes. Instead, they point to Biden, who left office last year in January.

Seated at the bar next to Ott is Rebecca Lashley, a retired nursing assistant who said Trump deserves the benefit of the doubt after Biden’s policies.

“It took Biden four years of screwing up. How’s [Trump] gonna fix it in two years?” Lashley asked.

“Do you realise what Biden left that man? He left that man a hell of a big plate”, he said.

It’s a familiar line frequently touted by the White House.

Since his return to power for a second presidential term in 2025, Trump and members of his administration have regularly claimed they aren’t to blame for the nation’s cost-of-living issues. In social media posts last month, the president wrote that “price increases throughout America were caused by Sleepy Joe Biden and the Biden Administration, not by ‘TRUMP.’”

“We’re coming out of years of energy subtraction,” US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a recent Fox News interview as he blamed the Biden administration for rising fuel prices.

Five hours south of Pennsylvania, in ruby red Amelia County, Virginia, Terry Williams largely agreed with Trump.

After cooking up a Sunday breakfast, the delivery driver sank deep into his well-worn, waterfall-back couch to prepare for a full afternoon of football viewing. But before the day’s first kickoff, he issued a blunt, expletive-laden rant about a “bullshit” economy that larger “deep state” forces were preventing the president from fixing.

“I think that Trump just [blames Biden] because he just can’t come out and tell people the truth,” the self-described “Trump-lican” said as smells of bacon grease emanated from his kitchen. “The reason why I say that is the Federal Reserve. Their answer to everything is to print money.”

“The Federal Reserve Bank, the stockholders of the Federal Reserve, whoever the hell these people are, they’re creating more currency because they don’t have no choice.”

Williams, who voiced support for Trump’s second-term pressure tactics on the Fed to lower interest rates, said policies created by the US central bank have left the country with currency that has no real intrinsic value.

“I just believe that this economy is an illusion and we’re using fake money,” he said.

After Trump campaigned on a promise to bring down stubborn inflation wrought by the pandemic, his second term has consisted of a range of broadly unpopular initiatives that have forced higher prices on much of the country.

His tariff policies, instituted during a “Liberation Day” event at the White House last year, have minimal support. The AP found that nearly 65 percent of Americans blame Trump’s policies for high costs.

The nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimates tariffs put in place under Trump resulted in an average tax increase of more than $1,000 for US households last year. After the US Supreme Court rendered most of the president’s tariffs illegal in January, that estimate is slightly lower at $820 for 2026.

The policy’s impact is felt even more acutely in Virginia, which, according to the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, has paid an estimated $6.2bn extra since Trump’s tariffs were implemented. That breaks down to just under $1,800 per family.

But some of the state’s MAGA voters, like Williams, say despite the extra cost, they “believe” in Trump’s tariff policy, arguing it should be expanded.

“I love the thought of a tariff system. That way, the American people do not get taxed,” Williams said. “I love that concept.”

But it is the war in Iran that could prove to be the most consequential for Trump and Republicans when Americans make their midterm picks.

As the conflict stretches into its eighth month, just 27 percent of registered US voters said last month that they approve of it, according to a New York Times/Siena poll. That number, however, is much higher among Trump’s most loyal supporters: 65 percent.

“If it needs to happen to save our republic, absolutely,” Williams said of Trump’s war on Iran. But he expressed unease at increasing petrol prices wrought by the president’s war.

Since the first US-Israeli attack on Iran was launched in late February, fuel prices in the US have skyrocketed. The national average for regular petrol is $4.29 a gallon (3.8 litres), up more than $1.30 from last September, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Trump has begun to acknowledge the war — and its resulting economic impacts — could cost his party control of Congress.

“Well, it’s possible,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. “Because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. So when you say, ‘Is it OK for Iran to have a nuclear weapon?’, I would say 100 percent of the people say ‘no’, including worldwide. So, when you say it that way, it would help. If you don’t say that, it could hurt.”

For the sake of US security, most MAGA voters say they’re willing to bear the cost of Trump’s Iran decision — and America, they believe, should, too.

“What would happen if he wouldn’t have done that? What would happen? Nothing good,” Lashley said. “We have to sacrifice to make things better. I don’t care who you are. We’re with him to make that sacrifice.”

Ott explained how the war’s higher fuel prices have forced changes to his landscaping business. He’s had to tack a fuel surcharge onto his customers’ bills and lay off more than a dozen employees.

“I don’t have a problem with it,” Ott said about the war. “I have a business, and I have to sacrifice.”

President Trump has repeatedly promised that Americans will eventually reap the rewards of his policies.

After launching what turned out to be a trade war with US allies, Trump last year promised to use tariff revenue to give Americans what he described as a $2,000 “dividend” payment.

“People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!” Trump posted to his Truth Social account on November 9, before adding, “A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.”

The Trump administration had refunded more than $100bn as of late August following the Supreme Court ruling. But that money went to businesses, not directly to ordinary Americans.

In the lead-up to the midterms, Trump has made promises of more cash payments. During his speech at the Republican National Committee midterm convention in September, the US president said US adults would receive a $5,000 “Trump dividend” if his party “wins” next month’s elections.

Polling indicates that proposal has backfired, with 45 percent of unaffiliated voters telling NBC News they would be less likely to support a candidate who’s in agreement with it.

But it plays well — extremely well, even — with Trump’s base, whose members believe they’re entitled to a form of compensation from the government.

“I think it’s great if the president can help all people that need it,” Lashley said. “I mean, we got the money. We all contributed in our life to our country.”

“I paid tax all my life. I deserve something back”, Ott said. “They never give me nothing.”

Lashley stood up and replied, “That’s right!”

Most Americans say Trump’s economic policies have burdened, rather than benefitted, them.

About seven in 10 Americans, including more than half of Republicans, believe his handling of the cost of living has been “worse than expected”, according to the AP poll.

But MAGA voters say they are sticking firmly with the president, even as his economic agenda faces growing criticism across the country.

To understand why his most hardcore supporters remain loyal, it is important to understand how Trump built his political coalition in the first place.

A study by New America found that Trump’s coalition has been closely bound and heavily driven by resentment towards opposing cultural and political groups. Lashley reflected that sentiment when she blamed immigrants for the country’s cost-of-living crisis.

“They’re taking over the businesses in our country. They’re taking everything,” she said. “I’m not on board with giving people who come here more than what we get. No!”

Lashley went even further, saying she wished Trump could remain president for the rest of his life.

“I wish he could be our president until he died,” she said. “What is going to happen when he’s gone? That’s what really worries me.”

Rising prices alone have not been enough to sever the bond between Trump and some of his most loyal voters.

For many of them, the choice is not simply between an expensive economy and a cheaper one. It is about what – and who – might come after Trump.

“I’m afraid that somebody’s going to get in there that’s not gonna do the job, and then we’re gonna go downhill again,” Ott said. “I worry about the Democrats”.

“Me too. They’re crazy,” Lashley replied.

“What they’re gonna do to this country. We’re gonna be suffering,” Ott said. “We might as well be living in South Africa or somewhere like that.”

That loyalty could prove important in November.

In this year’s Republican primaries, Trump has demonstrated that the GOP primary electorate will follow his lead. A string of victories by candidates he endorsed in the US states of Indiana, Kentucky and Texas has further solidified his grip on the party.

While the president’s political instinct for activating his loyal, but often low-propensity, voters in critical elections has generally been effective, it is less clear whether they can hold back a rising wave of Democratic support.

Progressive and liberal-leaning candidates have coalesced around a message of affordability and lower prices – an approach that has resonated with voters who feel increasingly squeezed by Trump’s policies.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in August showed that US voters gave Democrats a 36 to 28 percent advantage over Republicans on cost-of-living issues.

While Lashley acknowledged that the issue resonated with her, she said there were no circumstances in which she would consider voting against the president.

More than 70 percent of US voters who identify with MAGA indicated in a September PBS News/NPR/Marist poll that they were voting in this election to support Trump.

For Williams, who said he plans to vote a straight Republican ticket in November, the economy is not his priority. The choice, he said, boils down to a battle he described as good versus evil.

“Look at the s*** that they’re trying to shove down our kids’ throats with these drag shows and the gender changes,” Williams vented as he described some Democrats’ positions on transgender rights. “Now I don’t know about you, but that’s evil right there. And I have a huge problem with that.”

But Ott said he was sticking with Republicans because of his optimism that economic conditions in the US would improve during the second half of the president’s term.

“[Trump] is gonna do more,” he said. “This economy is going to be so much better.”
